Ruleborn · design document v3.6

Audit register

Everything that changed about the plan, and everything that still needs fixing in the document. Section marks point into the design document; the repository is the source of truth and this page is generated from it.

Read against version 3.6. Five versions have now answered this register, and each item carries what each one did, as a note per version beneath it. 111 items are fixed in the document itself — including where a fix stopped short.

v3.6 records the owner's designs, and closes nothing. Screens v3 — 28 screens, 43 character and creature sheets with 3D models, 393 icons — is the visual reference, and §23.5 lets the document win on every rule. Of the 19 items v3.6 touches, none closes: G28 and F37 narrow, and C11 reopens. Reading the designs against v3.6 and the build — twelve readers, each finding tried by an adversarial verifier — found 62 more; reading your design handoff's own notes and fix brief found 4, and folding it in found 2, v3.6 against itself; 42 of the 68 are decisions for you, now in the brief, and the rest are what stage SD of the roadmap builds. The designs add mechanics the document lacks (build timers, a shield on home, presence, quests), leave out things it requires (law pylons, the guard form), and set a visual language §21.8 does not have, which is the first of your new decisions.

v3.4 closes 15 of the 17 items it answers. Each was read against the built document by section and line rather than taken from §31.9's own list, every check that tracked one was re-run, and the rules it changed were ported to the simulation and the harness the same day. Two stay open, both waiting on the same economy re-run — C19, C35 — and that re-run is this repository's to do (D58 first). The four items registered after v3.4's snapshot (F33, F34, G17, D58) are not in its list.

Reading it against itself, and running the sweep it names, found 67 more. F35: brief 37's rule for the crack's reach cannot choose one, because with no call at all the depth gate fails from two realms up and every realm level holds far above its band — so its fallback would delete the call on evidence that says nothing about the call; read on its own, every metre of reach costs depth, and the 5 m shipped removes it. G18: a ward ignores its disarmer only while it stands on the tile, so a Well or a Glare still fires on the walk there. C40: one sentence §31.3's own change made false. And D59, the harness's own: its optimal crew disarmed what v3.3 made a fifteen-second job and played below the competent crew, which every depth figure on v3.3's wards measured.

Before that, v3.3 closed 55 of 64; reading v3.3 against itself and porting it found F32 to F34, and the server found G17 and D58.

120 edits are drafted across 68 items — the section to open, the sentence as it stands today, and what to put there. Every quoted sentence is checked against the document by tools/check_edits.py, which fails the build if one is not there or appears twice.

The first three bars measure the audit: an item is settled when the document answers it. 46 items need both sides and count on both, so those two add up to more than 290.

The last three answer a different question — when can the drawing start? Each counts only the items that decide something its designer would otherwise have to guess, so 100% means that area can begin, not that the project is done. Nothing has been drawn yet; these say what each area is waiting on, and the panel above lists every gate by name.

What is blocked, and why

139 items are open. Each is counted once, by how critical it is and by the one thing holding it — 46 wait on a decision of yours. Read from the register itself (what each item waits on, the reason it has no edit, the edits drafted for it), so this cannot say something is moving that is not. The topic is the design chapter the item is filed under.

What is built

The simulation core in sim/, read from the last run of its own gate rather than from anything typed here. A system reads built only if every test that proves it passed; a test that is renamed or deleted makes its system read proof missing, never built.

27/27systems built
204/204tests passing
5/5golden replays verify
1269bytes, largest heist of 2,048

Systems

  • Built Fixed-point arithmetic §24.7 · T3.1 · 6/6 tests64-bit with 32 fractional bits for positions, 32-bit with 16 for angles. No floating point anywhere in the simulation.
  • Built Angles and trigonometry §24.7 · T3.1 · 4/4 testsAngles as a fraction of a turn, sine from a committed table computed in exact decimal arithmetic.
  • Built Seeded randomness §24.7 · T3.1 · 3/3 testsSplitMix64 into xoshiro256++, one stream per subsystem so one subsystem's draws cannot shift another's.
  • Built The tick and its checksum §24.10 · T3.1 · 4/4 testsSix phases in a fixed order; a checksum every tick, one a second kept, sensitive to one unit in the last place.
  • Built Replay format §24.10 · T3.2 · 7/7 testsCommands, never state. A header pinning 24.11's four things, a varint command log, and a four-byte checksum a second, under 2 KB.
  • Built Golden replays §24.11 · T3.2 · 2/2 testsHeists encoded by an earlier build and committed; every build re-simulates them and names the second any divergence starts at.
  • Built Tile grid §12.18 · T5.5 · 4/4 testsPer-tile terrain and continuous positions; 5.2's realm sizes; a fixed north-east-south-west neighbour order.
  • Built Pathfinding §12.18 · T5.5 · 7/7 testsBreadth-first, ties by tile index. Terrain slows the walk and cannot bend the route.
  • Built Crew control §12.18 · T5.5 · 2/2 testsThe crew never makes a decision the player did not make: no re-routing, no different door, friends pass through one another.
  • Built Line of sight §12.17 · T5.2 · 12/12 testsPer tile, as 21.12 requires. Feet and eyes are separate properties, as 6.2's fence and fog bank require. The same line from either end. What a guard's cone reaches is drawn from the same rule, tile by tile (21.12).
  • Built Noise §12.17 · T5.2 · 4/4 testsSound travels along the walkable path, never through walls: a guard turns toward the way around, not toward the source. The document's five carrying distances, in steps a crew would walk.
  • Built Guard states §12.17 · T5.2 · 5/5 testsUnaware, Suspicious, Investigating, Alerted, Searching, Returning, at the document's thresholds. No fall-back inside half a second; ten seconds searching the spot, twenty after losing sight, then home. Nothing random in it: §12.17 promises a scouting player can predict exactly what will happen.
  • Built Realm alarm §12.17 · T5.2 · 3/3 testsAn alert reaches guards within four metres half a second later; the realm alarm climbs once every thirty seconds to six; at five one more Warden arrives at the entrance.
  • Built Detection modifiers §12.17 · T5.2 · 6/6 testsThe corner of the eye at half the rate; crouched halves, running adds three quarters, an unlit tile halves again, multiplied once; still in tall grass is invisible until a guard walks into the tile; gravel and water carry sound further, moss less.
  • Built Roles and gaits §11.1 · T5.5 · 3/3 testsCrew and guards move at §11.1's speed for their role, over any number of tile edges. Walk, crouch or run by command; the two gait speeds are the simulation's reading, since the document gives neither.
  • Built The Vault and loading §12.19 · T5.5 · 7/7 tests1,500 health a Vault level, cracked from beside it one hit every 0.8 s, Breakers for double and a quarter more while two or more work it (the assist bonus, v3.3); no guard hears the Vault, as the owner decided (F35): v3.4's hit noise and its call every five seconds of cracking are gone, and a guard beside it still sees the crew. Once open, every crew member loads at 30 a second to the fill the player set, until the bag is full or the exposed share is gone — a full crew in ten seconds. A loaded Carrier walks 15% slower.
  • Built Fights, knockouts and capture §12.20 · T5.5 · 10/10 testsOne hit every 0.8 s for Power, on both sides. An ambush on a guard that has not noticed the crew is a two-second takedown and a knockout, whatever the roles (v3.3); a guard that notices first takes an ordinary hit, and an open hit sends it to 1000. A body is seen as a still crew member lying on its tile would be, and can be dragged at crouching speed. A crew member at zero health drops its loot and is caught in ten seconds unless an ally revives it (3 s, a Mender 1.5). A knocked-out guard found by another raises the realm alarm.
  • Built The skiff, the clock and the outcome §12.9 · T5.5 · 6/6 testsThe skiff comes to an edge tile in 20 s at the Heart and takes whoever holds the spot; anyone inside when the clock ends is caught. §12.9's four grades from who got out with what. A heist planned as a player would play it ends Clean with every bag full. Loading stops when the clock left no longer covers getting out; dropping loot costs exactly the fraction dropped.
  • Built Landing §5.4 · T5.5 · 5/5 testsThe crew lands where the raider chooses: a landing in the input log, at tick 0, puts the whole crew on one open edge tile before any other input of that tick. Guards within 6 tiles of the spot, walked as every sound travels (§12.17), start at 250 of 1,000 suspicion unless it is in fog, darkness or tall grass. Ghost tide returns a knocked-out crew member to the landing spot. A late, second or inland landing is dropped, and the server refuses a heist that never lands. An island needs one open edge tile, and a walkable route from some open edge tile to the Vault; `Island::landings` lists the tiles a crew may choose. The Heart's no-landing rule waits for universes of several realms.
  • Built Laws and pylons §12.21 · T5.3 · 31/31 testsAll 48 laws as exact ratios, generated from content/law_effects.json. Each tick the rule sheet is the product of the laws whose pylons stand: speed, sight, suspicion, noise, structure and fight damage, alarm range, the clock, Glass and Stillness. A pylon broken — 600 health, Breakers double — switches its law off from the next tick and earns its page. A replay's rules field is a digest of the laws it was made under. Kinship and Regrowth heal once a second, each with its own parameter (F31); Regrowth heals wards too. v3.4's other rows (§7.3) are parameters as well, so the launch 24 are whole: friction off and a wall's rebound (Frictionless, Bounce), health and speed read by size (Density), a triggered effect landing late (Delay), sight in a moving band (Aurora), a hit's jump (Chain lightning), a stun on touch (Static), Revival's return and swap shapes, the highest applying once (Echoes, Soul swap), touch damage (Thorns) and a cut hedge regrowing (Bloom). Where the document leaves the rule open, the reading is G23's.
  • Built Resonances and chords §8 · T5.3 · 37/37 tests§8's four kinds of combination, worked out each tick from the laws whose pylons stand, so a broken pylon silences every one its law was part of. Harmonies strengthen the shared kind of effect on both laws — movement, slowing, damage and stuns, healing and regrowth, returns — by a quarter, and Glow and Hush lengthen light and hiding by their tiles. Dissonances add their unpredictable effect from the heist's own seeded stream: gusts, flicker, wildfire, déjà vu. The twelve signature resonances that ship at launch and all twelve chords each change the rule they name. The laws' notes, the resonance pairs and the chords' notes are generated from content, and the rules version covers them. What each combination costs in stability is the economy's, and where §8 stops short of a rule the reading is G25's.
  • Built Wards §10.3 · T5.5 · 13/13 testsAll six of §10.3's wards at level 1, as spec/wards.md reads them: Crystal Wall and Thorn Hedge passive, Static Coil an aura, Gravity Well, Time Snare and Lantern Glare triggered by the first crew member in reach and then resetting. Lantern Glare fires within 2 tiles (v3.3). A ward can be disarmed standing on its tile — fifteen seconds at every level, silent, restarting if the disarmer steps off; the ward's sensor ignores the one on its tile disarming it and fires on anyone else (v3.4), but not on the walk there (G18) — or smashed, loudly, Breakers double.
  • Built Height §12.17 · T5.2 · 4/4 tests§6.2's raised ground, 0 to 3 levels: climbing one needs a ramp, stairs or vines, or Honeycomb or Half gravity; dropping is free and one-way, and is heard — 2 m from one level, 4 m from three. A guard a level up sees a metre further per level; one looking up loses its far zone.
  • Built Island bundles §24.8 · T3.3 · 4/4 testsAn island as one canonical encoding, addressed by its SHA-256; refused if it is any other encoding. The fixture realm and a legal example Heart are bundles, and every world is built from one.
  • Built Publishing rules §5.2 · T3.3 · 3/3 tests5.2's ward limit, guard posts and law slots by realm level, one thing a tile, an open edge tile to land on and at least half of each side open (F51, decided), and 6.1's route to the Vault from some open edge tile with every Crystal Wall standing. A builder edits an island through `Island`'s own methods — ground features, posts, wards, woven laws and their pylons, the Vault — each keeping it an island the format can write, and `check` alone says whether it may be published.
  • Built Rules version and the validator §24.11 · T3.3 · 4/4 testsThe rules version is a hash of the law table and this build's behaviour on the golden heists, so it moves by itself; the validator re-simulates a replay on the island and rules its header names and returns the re-simulation's outcome.
  • Built Eras §18.3 · T5.3 · 10/10 testsThe week's era, first on the rule sheet (§7.3): The Long Night's shorter sight, Glass Moon's see-through walls, Heavy Stars holding Half gravity down, Wildgrowth's stronger Life laws, Echoing Skies as a Revival source, Static Storm's stronger coil and Quiet Week's longer clock. The era travels in the replay (RBH2, one byte; RBH1 unchanged for none) and the table is in the rules version.

The simulation against content/

157 values the simulation carries as constants agree with detection.json, roles.json and, for the numbers with no content file, tools/design_facts.py. Every other number in those files is named below as not modelled yet, and the gate fails on any it neither compares nor names — so none passes as agreeing by being absent. Last come the numbers the simulation needs that the document does not give.

  • Not modelled noise.off_screen_multiplier — the simulation has no screen
  • Not modelled ambush.level_advantage_cap — every character is level 1: there are no levels yet
  • Not modelled rule sheet unlit_drain — Soul lanterns: needs lantern light, an object not built
  • Not modelled rule sheet carry_weight — no law sets it
  • Not modelled rule sheet cone_angle — no law sets it
  • Not in the document LandingTwo = 6 half metres — landing from two levels, 3 m; §12.17 gives one level (2 m) and three (4 m) and nothing between
  • Not in the document GLARE_BLIND_TICKS = 60 — Lantern Glare's blind, read as the crew unable to act; §10.3 says "blinds them" and not what a blinded crew cannot do
  • Not in the document AURORA_BAND_ROWS = 2 — Aurora's band, two rows deep, one crossing the realm a period; §7.4 says "bands of light sweep the realm every 10 seconds" and not how wide a band is or how many there are (G23)
  • Not in the document DEJA_VU_WINDOW_TICKS = None — Déjà vu comes in the minute after the clash first sounds; §8.3 says "once per heist" and not when (G25)
  • Not in the document BURN_DAMAGE = (5, 100) — Wildfire hurts 5% of full health a second, the Thorn Hedge's rate; §8.3 says the flames are "hurting anyone inside" and not by how much (G25)
  • Not in the document MUFFLED_STEPS = 1 — Deep sleep's muffled footstep carries a step less; §8.5 says "flowers muffle footsteps" and not how much (G25)
  • Not in the document FAIR_LIGHTS_TICKS = 600 — Fair lights forms an illusion every 20 seconds; §8.5 gives no cadence; 20 s is its neighbours' (G25)
  • Not in the document QUICKSAND_PITS = 3 — Quicksand opens three pits; §8.5 says "a few tiles" (G25)
  • Not in the document PIT_HOLD_TICKS = 30 — a pit holds whoever falls in for a second; §8.5 says a pit drops anyone a level and not what that costs (G25)

    The four chains that carry most of the graph

    The generator. C5 and Q8 settle how many guard posts a realm has → F22 → F11 → F9 and F13. Nothing downstream is fixable by improving the generator alone.

    The raid payout. C4 says what §9.6’s level term is → C2 picks one model → F14 re-derives the 0.46 the progression curve rests on → F19 turns it into a band.

    Law rarity. C8 settles the Library, which now decides the page economy → Q3 → C3 → C23.

    Scope. F10 classifies the 48 laws by what each needs from the engine → D6 → Q5 → G11.

    What cannot be settled from inside this repository — 11 questions

    Everything else here is arithmetic against the design document or a measurement the simulation harness can make. These are not: each needs a number from the outside world. Each is written to stand alone.

    1. C12 The high revenue scenario quietly uses a different commission rateWhat are the current Apple and Google commission tiers and the revenue thresholds that move a developer between them, and what does that do to a revenue band either side of the boundary? §22.2’s high scenario is computed at a different rate from the other two and §22.5 does not say so.
    2. C20 The 48 law sound signatures are six school sounds repeatedWhat does a per-school sound set cost against a per-law one, and do players in comparable games actually distinguish audio cues at that granularity? §21.8 now claims six school signatures where it once claimed 48.
    3. C29 v3.0 removed the playtesters and kept two phase gates that require themHow do small teams recruit ten to twenty playtesters for a pre-release mobile build, what does it cost, and what consent and privacy position does handling pre-release content with outside testers require? §26.2 gates two phases on those people and §25.4 says they do not exist.
    4. D6 A launch-scope cut of roughly 40% is proposedWhich of a launch content set actually drives retention in this genre: breadth of distinct rules, or depth in a few? The proposed cut halves the laws and keeps the Island Workshop, and nothing outside this repository has been consulted about that trade.
    5. D9 Iteration is given a budgetWhat is the reference-class ratio of iteration work to first-build work for a novel genre blend with no reference implementation? §26.8 estimates ~270 agent runs to build and then states that the iteration needed to find the fun is unbudgeted.
    6. F10 Sixteen of forty-eight laws are parameter changes; the rest need an engine featureWhat does each kind of law effect really cost to build — a parameter change against a spawned entity against a periodic rule — on a deterministic fixed-tick mobile simulation? `scope_cut.py` weights them 0 / 3 / 2 by judgement, and the ordering is what the conclusion rests on.
    7. F13 §12.22’s matchmaking guarantee has no targets to draw from earlyHow do comparable games fill a matchmaking band when the candidate pool cannot supply it — bots, staged targets, widening, or something else? §12.22 promises a median target in a band that does not exist early.
    8. G11 Localisation of a coined vocabulary has no ownerWhat does it cost to localise a coined vocabulary — roughly 130 invented proper nouns — into twelve languages, and who normally owns that work on a team of this size? §26.3 assigns nobody.
    9. Q5 Accept the launch-scope cut?How much content do comparable mobile builders actually ship at launch, counted the way §26.1 counts — distinct rules, creature forms, building types, languages — and how much did they add per season afterwards? §26.1 asks a team of one designer, one coding agent and three contractors for 48 laws, 144 creature forms, 39 terrain features and 12 languages.
    10. Q6 Casual pacing: leave it, or add the catch-up discount?How do comparable games handle a player who is years behind the curve, and does a visible, openly labelled catch-up discount hold up in practice? §27.5 settles on one and never specifies it, against a finishing time of roughly 1,343 days.
    11. Q7 The document's own open listTrade-mark clearance for the name, in the launch territories. §26.9 makes it a gate on any public use and it costs nothing to start.

An item can be settled for one area and open for another — C6 stopped deciding anything a character artist draws when v3.1 reconciled the two rosters’ roles, and still decides which ability text a screen shows.

    What changed about the approach

    Deviations from the plan the design document sets out, each with what it costs and why it was worth it.

    D1

    The build-willingness test runs first, not second

    change Adopted backend
    §26.7§13.3§30.8

    §26.7 schedules the paper heist first and the build-willingness test after it. But the build test is ranked risk #1, and §26.7 itself calls it “the single decision that changes the most”. The heist test decides whether the game is fun; the build test decides what game is being built — authorship, authorship-with-scaffolding, or a pivot to generated islands the player curates.

    → Run both in parallel. Neither blocks the other, and the build test's answer changes what the rest of the plan is for.

    D2

    The paper prototype became a browser prototype

    change Done backend
    §19.27§26.7§25.4

    Both pre-code gates as written assume about thirty people in a room — eight to twelve for the paper heist, fifteen to twenty for the build test. That cohort does not exist for this project. The questions did not change; the method did, because a link can be sent to strangers and a room cannot. v2.3’s §25.5 — renumbered §25.4 in v3.1 — budgeted for recruited remote panels, so the route was costed. That sentence is no longer in the document: v3.0 rewrote the section to rule panels out, which is what D20 and C29 are about.

    → Built and published. It also answers a question paper could not: whether a delegated crew feels like playing or watching (§30.7 premise 3), which cannot be tested on a board where a human moves the pieces.

    v3.0 Overtaken. §19.27 now answers every pre-code question by simulation rather than by people, so the published prototype is no longer on the critical path. It still runs, and it is still the only artefact that can answer the one question §19.27 says simulation cannot. See D20.

    D3

    The prototype sits ahead of the determinism spike on the critical path

    change Adopted backend
    §26.7§24.2§26.5

    §26.7 puts the determinism spike immediately after the paper tests. Because the paper test became software, a few working sessions of engineering now precede the spike — exactly what the paper test was designed to avoid.

    → Accepted: §26.5's own rule is that scope is the lever, and buying the two project-deciding answers cheaply is worth it. This does not relax the rule that gameplay code waits for the spike. The prototype is throwaway and written as such.

    D4

    A reconciliation step was inserted before the specification locks

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §26.7

    waits on C1, C2, C3, C5, C6

    §26.7 goes spike → lock the simulation contract → lock detection → lock the law schema → lock saves. Every one of those assumes there is one specification to lock. Four systems currently have two (C1, C2, C3, C6), and a fifth has two budgets (C5).

    → Work the blocking half of this register before any lock. It is days of desk time and the cheapest work in the whole plan.

    v3.1 Closed. §31.8 schedules reconciliation ahead of §26.7’s locks and calls it a gate rather than a milestone — which is what this item asked for, in the document’s own voice.

    D5

    The economy model was rebuilt from scratch

    change Done backend
    §24§10.2§14.2§14.3§9.3

    §24 describes a Python model that generated roughly a quarter of the document's numbers. That model is not in the document, so none of those numbers could be re-derived or re-tuned (gap G7).

    → Rebuilt at tools/economy_model/. It reproduces the first month to within 10% and the Keeper curve to within three days, and it produced findings F1, F2 and F3.

    D6

    A launch-scope cut of roughly 40% is proposed

    change Fixed in the document both
    §26.1§26.5§26.8§30.8

    waits on F10 · unblocks Q5

    §26.1's launch table asks for 48 laws, 144 creature forms, 44 resonances, 39 terrain features, 16 buildings, 27 screens and 12 languages, from one designer, one coding agent and three contractors. §26.5 says scope discipline is the main risk control and §30.8 ranks execution as risk #2 — but neither is applied to §26.1.

    → Proposed: 24 laws rather than 48 (the Codex already gates in chapters); 3 form-notes rather than 8; ~20 resonances rather than 44; 2–3 languages rather than 12 (§20.6 already says this); constellations to v1.1; wards at 2 levels rather than 5. The Island Workshop is the one thing not to cut — it is the only credible answer to the content treadmill at this team size.

    v3.3 Decided: the cut is taken. §26.1 ships 24 laws “chosen by engine cost”, 54 forms, 12 signature resonances, two ward levels and two languages, with constellations in version 1.1 and the Workshop kept. The 24 are a rule rather than a choice (§7.10), and check_document now re-derives them from the 48 sheets: the rule, the badges, the table and the engine-point totals (78, 14, and 36 for a 24 chosen by rank) all agree.

    D7

    A risk was added: delegated control reading as watching

    change Adopted backend
    §30.7§30.8§19.4

    §30.7 marks premise 3 — that delegated control still feels like agency — as only conditionally supported, names the failure mode (“my units are stupid”), and sets a 70% felt-control threshold. It does not appear in §30.8's ranked register. Meanwhile §19.4 concedes performative challenge is “almost absent by design”, and the system that decides it — pathfinding and crew control — is the largest specification gap (G1).

    → Added at rank ~4. The prototype measures it directly.

    D8

    Two risks were re-ranked

    change Adopted backend
    §30.8§19.4§20.10

    Trust and safety moved from 6 to 8: the design has already engineered most of that risk away — no free text for minors, no uploads, structured data only, preset chat. Complexity overwhelming new players moved from 7 to 6: §19.4 calls it “the biggest risk in the whole design” and the four-interacting-rules cap is untested.

    → No action beyond ordering the mitigations accordingly.

    D9

    Iteration is given a budget

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §26.8§19.17§26.5

    §26.8 estimates ~270 agent runs (≈810 focused hours) and then states plainly that the iteration needed to find the fun is unbudgeted. For a novel genre blend with no reference implementation, that iteration is normally the majority of the work. §19.17 alone lists nine A/B experiments, each needing a playable build and a tuning pass.

    → Budget iteration at 1–1.5× the build estimate (a further 200–400 runs) and treat the total as the reference-class figure §26.5 asks for.

    v3.3 §26.8 budgets iteration as its own line at 1× the build, a floor: 229 to 405 runs, plan total 458 to 810, about 640. The arithmetic re-derives.

    D10

    The document should split into a specification and a research archive

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §19§28§30

    The document is a buildable spec and an evidence archive in one file, and §19, §28 and §30 are roughly 40% of the text. Both halves are valuable. Keeping them together means the spec cannot be read, diffed or implemented without the archive — and it is part of why four systems reached v2.3 specified twice.

    → docs/design/spec/ carries decisions, one file per system; docs/design/research/ carries why. Cross-reference, never duplicate. Started: spec/detection.md is the first file, and the twelve content tables in content/ are the data half of the same split.

    v3.1 Closed. §31.2 splits the repository four ways — /spec for decisions, /data for numbers, /archive for reasoning, /build for output that nobody edits — which is this item’s proposal with a fourth compartment it did not think of: the generated one.

    D11

    The prototype departs from the document's numbers on purpose

    change Done backend
    §12.6§12.8§12.17§5.4

    Vault health is 600 rather than 1,500 so cracking takes about eight seconds; being caught takes 1.6 seconds of contact and takes one crew member at a time; there are two guards; the island is hand-built. The first build caught all three crew instantly, which read as unfair rather than tense and would have produced a false negative on gate 1.

    → Prototype-only. None of these numbers carries forward. The catch-takes-time change is worth considering for the real build, because instant total capture conflicts with §12.14's rule that failure stays temporary.

    D12

    The published prototype declares no runtime capabilities

    change Adopted backend
    §13.3§25.4

    Server-side result collection would have been convenient, but declaring the database capability makes an artifact organisation-internal and unshareable publicly — which defeats the entire point of recruiting by link.

    → Results are collected in the browser and shown as a copyable code. tools/parse_gate_results.py scores them.

    D13

    The note distribution should be rebalanced before the law table is authored

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §8.1§7.4§24

    unblocks C25, D14

    Parsed from all 48 law sheets: Glow is carried by 12 laws, its opposite Hush by 6. Hush is the hiding note — the raider-favouring one — and it is the scarcest, while the revealing note is the most abundant. Since laws are woven by the defender and apply symmetrically, defenders have both the least reason and the fewest options to weave Hush. Five of the twelve chords require it.

    → Rebalance toward roughly 8–9 laws per note. §24 freezes the note count at eight and makes laws the expansion axis, so this is a one-time cost now and a permanent constraint on every future season's six laws.

    v3.0 Claimed, not done — and now written out. §8.8 states “The table now runs eight or nine laws per note”. Parsing all 48 law sheets gives Glow 12, Flow 11, Echo 10, Weight 9, Spark 8, Bloom 8, Veil 7, Hush 6 — unchanged from v2.3 (C25).

    tools/note_rebalance.py is the change that paragraph describes, law by law: nine edits reach nine laws for every note, each argued from §8.1’s own definition rather than chosen to make the arithmetic work. Flock and Crystal growth give up Glow for Veil because neither lights up and both transform; Aurora gives up Flow because it moves nothing; Day and night gains Hush because the light-and-dark law carried neither Glow nor Hush.

    The tool refuses to emit a proposal that puts two opposite notes on one law — which it caught in the first draft, where Aurora would have carried Glow and Hush — and checks that every chord stays reachable afterwards. All twelve do, at unchanged cost.

    v3.3 Nine laws were re-noted. Opposite pairs are within two laws of each other, no law carries a note and its opposite, and every chord stays reachable.

    D15

    Summary tables are now generated, not authored

    change Done backend
    §11.2§7.4§29.1§24.9

    unblocks C21, C6

    Four register items — C1, C3, C6 and C19 — have one cause: the same facts written down twice by hand, and one copy updated. The structural fix is that a table which exists only to summarise something else is never authored, only emitted.

    → tools/generate_docs.py emits §11.2's roster index, §7.4's law summary and §29.1's formulas appendix from content/. --check fails the build if a generated file has been hand-edited, and ./tools/check_all.sh runs it. This matters most for §29.1, which still carries the detection model §12.17 superseded — the worst place for a stale number, since it is where an implementer looks for it. It does not cover prose, which is what D10's split is for.

    v3.0 Vindicated in the worst way. §30.18 draws exactly this conclusion — “a table that exists only to summarise something else should be generated, never authored” — and then v3.0 fixed six systems and left stale copies of four of them (C21–C23, C6). §29.1 is the sharpest case: it is the formulas appendix, it carries the detection model §12.8 deleted, and it cites §12.8 as its source.

    D14

    Chords should require three laws, not three notes

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §8.5

    waits on D13 · unblocks F23

    §8.5 calls chords “the late-game discovery” needing “three laws in play and a Lab of level 3”. Because 23 of the 48 laws carry two notes, all twelve chords are reachable with two laws, several with two commons. Slow rivers + Whispers gives Iron bell for 26 stability — inside a day-2 player's capacity of 51.

    → Require three distinct laws. It is a one-line rule change and it preserves the stated design intent; the alternatives are to reposition chords as a mid-game discovery, or to reduce two-note laws (which also helps D13).

    v3.0 §8.8 changes the rule to three distinct laws, which makes §8.5 true. It did not achieve what it argued for: the cheapest chord now costs 33 stability against a day-2 capacity of 51, up from 26, and seven of twelve are still three commons. The gate that actually makes a chord late-game is the Lab level 3 at Spire 5, about day 42 — which §8.5 mentions and §8.8 does not lean on.

    v3.3 v3.3 re-noted nine laws (D13), and its §8.8 reads the chord rule less strictly than this repository’s validator did: a law may carry a note opposite to one in the chord, so long as each law contributes one of its three. By the document’s reading the cheapest chord costs 32 (Bloom, Brittle stone and Tilt, as §8.8 says) and 8 of the 12 can be completed by three commons. What makes chords late now is §8.5’s draw of 192 stability (F23), not the table.

    D28

    The job that keeps the playable build current ran, reported success, and published nothing

    change Done backend
    §30.18§26.7§19.27

    The prototype is the only artefact anyone outside this repository can actually touch, so an hourly Routine republishes it when the branch moves. It fired, took fifty-eight seconds, and was recorded SUCCEEDED. The published page did not change. Two faults, either one fatal on its own.

    It could not tell new from old. The job compared the prototype’s last commit date against the artifact’s publish date, and Artifact action: "list" reports only a calendar day. A commit and a publish on the same day are indistinguishable — so from the first day the two coincided, which was the day it was written, the job would have answered already current for ever.

    It could not publish. Artifact action: "read" saves the live page to a file and counts the version as viewed only once every line of it has been read. The prompt said to read it; it did not say that a partial read does not count. So the read was partial, the publish was refused, and the turn ended without error.

    The second is the same shape as D24–D26 wearing different clothes, and it is the one worth keeping: a job that cannot fail cannot be trusted when it passes. Nothing threw, so nothing was reported, so the artifact sat a day behind the code while the dashboard read green.

    → Both fixed. The page now carries a BUILD stamp — a digest of itself with that line removed — so the job compares the published page against the current page instead of comparing two dates: is the published page this page? build_prototype.py --stamp prints it, --self-test proves it still moves when the page moves, and both are build gates. The prompt now spells out the full-read requirement, and a final step requires the publish to report a new version number before the run may claim to have worked.

    Generalised since: tools/build_stamp.py stamps all three published pages — the prototype, this register and the roadmap — and holds each one’s path and artifact URL, so the job reads what to publish rather than carrying a hard-coded list. The prototype keeps its stamp as a JavaScript constant because it shows it on screen; the two generated pages carry an HTML comment. One digest function strips either form, because two implementations of a stamp would be the very fault this register exists to record.

    The general rule, alongside D27’s: an automated job needs a check that its work landed, not just that it ran.

    D32

    Both ability tables hand a crew two to three times the decisions §12.6 budgets for the whole run

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §12.6§12.5§11.2§11.11

    §12.6 sets the game’s pace in its own words: “a string of small, tense decisions: roughly one every 8 to 12 seconds, or 15 to 25 in a run… never about tapping faster”, and it names “when to use abilities and casts” as one of the decisions it is counting.

    An ability comes off cooldown every c seconds per character, so a crew of n over a clock of t gets t×n/c windows. §12.5 puts the crew at 3, 4 from Keeper 8 and 5 from Keeper 16, and the clock at 150 to 240 seconds. Against §11.11’s median 18-second cooldowns that is 25 windows at the smallest and 67 at the largest; against §11.2’s median 14, 31 and 83.

    So the smallest case in the document — a crew of three on a short route — exactly reaches the top of §12.6’s budget, and every case above it overruns. The overrun is not a tuning miss; it grows with the player. The crew goes 3 to 5 and the clock 150 to 240 as Keeper levels rise, so the game gets roughly two and a half times more frantic between Keeper 1 and Keeper 16, and §12.6 describes the first of those and not the second.

    For one ability to come off cooldown at §12.6’s own 8-to-12-second cadence, cooldowns would have to be 24–36 seconds at a crew of three and 40–60 at a crew of five. Both tables are 8–24.

    → Answer one question and all eighteen cooldowns follow from it: is using an ability one of the decisions §12.6 is counting, or is it texture between them?

    A decision. Cooldowns go to roughly 24 to 60 seconds and scale with crew size, so a character’s ability fires once or twice in a heist and choosing the moment is the point. §12.6’s count stands as written. This is the reading its own words support.

    Texture. Keep the short cooldowns and rewrite §12.6’s count to be about routes, pylons and greed, with abilities explicitly outside it. Then say what stops the phone becoming a tapping game, which §12.6 currently rules out in the same paragraph.

    Either way the number is one decision rather than eighteen, which is why C6’s drafted abilities settle the effects and leave the cooldowns here. tools/ability_text.py --self-test pins the overrun, so a re-cost that brings a table inside the budget fails the build and sends someone back to this item.

    v3.3 Decided by uses rather than longer cooldowns: two a heist, a ten-second lockout, six to ten ability choices a crew whatever the clock.

    chords = 12       4 homes
    terrain = 39      4 homes

Two of the thirteen were only visible once the strong rule ran, because §14.2 and §14.3 state the total and the milestones, so a per-section rule had counted them clean.

    D42

    The guard written for D41 found the same bug in a second extractor, on its first run

    change Done backend
    §31.2§31.4§11.7§11.11

    D41 was a law sheet whose block ran to the end of the document, so a column heading from §21.7 landed in §7.7’s content. The fix was one line of bounding; the interesting question was what else that shape had done.

    A general guard for it: every extracted value has to be inside the section it was read from. That is independent of how the extractor pairs cells, which is the part that keeps going wrong — fields() and table() both zip by position, so one stray cell shifts every row after it, and a shifted value almost always comes from outside its own section.

    It found a second one immediately. content/ruleborn.json gave Soulmender a look of “The Archivist” — a Sage’s name from §11.7. §11.11 says “Hooded moth-like spirit”. Same cause exactly: Soulmender is the eighteenth and last creature in the bible, its block was unbounded, and a later | Look pair overwrote it.

    Two extractors, the same last-block bug, one field wrong in each. Both files are read by every tool in this repository and both were wrong for as long as the extraction has existed.

    The two guards catch different things, which is why there are two. D41’s bad value was the label “How characters move”, which is inside §7.7 — provenance would have passed it, and the label check catches it. D42’s was a sentence from another section — the label check passes it, and provenance catches it. Neither is the whole net.

    → Fixed. Both extractors bound their last block at the next section heading, and re-extracting changes exactly one field in each: Mirror images’ world signature and Soulmender’s look, both to what the document says.

    validate_content.check_provenance() declares where each of the twelve content files is read from and refuses a value that is not there. Two kinds of exception are named rather than filtered: the keys this repository adds to the document’s content — which register item a row waits on, what the document does not state about it — and the files with two sources, which are ruleborn.json (§11.11’s bible plus the columns §11.2 adds) and buildings.json, where the Library is in §10.4 instead of §10.2 and being outside §10.2 is C8.

    Ten of the twelve files came back clean on the first run, which is the useful half of the result: the extraction is sound apart from a bug that only ever bites the last row, and now there is something that would say so.

    D34

    The clock D25 made readable reaches one crew of three, and for that one it is a wall rather than a price

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §5.4§12.19§12.6§13.2

    D25 found that no policy in tools/heist_harness/ read heist.clock, so shortening §5.4’s clock could kill a crew outright but never change what one chose to do — and nothing priced in time could be measured at all. The reading was added. Nothing checked what reading it did.

    Re-running D25’s own experiment against the fix: a competent crew with watches_clock on banks exactly what the same crew with it off banks, at every clock length tested — 24.1, 22.4 and 22.4 at 100%, 70% and 55%, the same mean to the decimal. _out_of_time needs the inbound journey to be long against what is left, and a crew that does not hold at checkpoints never gets there. A value that is read and changes nothing is indistinguishable from one that is not read, which is D25’s own lesson and D26’s.

    The one crew it reaches is the optimal one, which holds for cones, arrives late, and then aborts loading altogether: 20.9 mean fill at the full clock, 1.1 at 70% and 0.0 at 55%. Not less loot for less time — none.

    §12.19 asks for a dial: “loading longer earns more and the alarm clock is the price”, with the break-even at about 70% full “the dial for the game’s emotional peak”. A no-op is not a price and a cliff is not a price. So the number that sentence rests on is still not measurable, two fixes after D25 said so.

    → The stopping rule has to trade fill against time rather than switch on it. _out_of_time is a boolean — leave now if the way home is longer than what is left — and a boolean can only ever produce all or nothing.

    Make it a target rather than a trigger. The crew loads to whatever fill the remaining clock affords, at §12.19’s 30 units a second, and leaves with that. Then cutting the clock cuts the haul smoothly, §12.19’s sentence becomes true of the model, and the 70% break-even becomes something a sweep can find rather than a number the document asserts.

    Until then, treat every result computed across clock lengths as measuring a wall. test_the_clock_reaches_only_the_crew_that_cannot_use_it pins both halves, so neither can be fixed quietly or broken quietly.

    F8 is not affected, and that is worth saying. Its claim — runs finish with a third of the clock unused — holds under the competent crew (0.36 of the clock used) more strongly than under the optimal one (0.61), so it is not an artefact of a crew that gives up. F21 is not affected either: the optimal crew coming home empty is the polarisation F21 records and its test already asserts.

    v3.3 Decided in the text: the harness crew loads to a target, and the clock experiment passes only if mean fill falls as the clock shortens, with stated fallbacks. The measurement has not run; §32.9 carries it.

    D31

    §7.9’s two dials are one dial, measured across all 48 law sheets

    change Fixed in the document backend
    §7.1§7.9§7.7§12.4§12.5

    §7.9 is titled Rarity buys specificity, not strength and states the rule the whole rank system exists to enforce: “rarity governs how long a law takes to get, while stability cost and conditions govern how strong it is. These are two dials, and the earlier version tied them together.” §7.1 restates it as a property of every law: “Rank sets how long a law takes to acquire — not how strong it is.”

    Across the 48 sheets, rank predicts stability cost at r = +0.80. In 732 of 828 cross-rank pairs (88%) the rarer law costs more. The medians climb with the ladder: common 14, uncommon 17, rare 17, deep 22. Rank predicts conditions — the other dial §7.9 names — at r = −0.04, which is nothing, and common laws carry marginally more conditional text than rare ones. So v2.0 split the ranks and the sheets tied them back together.

    §7.9’s own remedy makes it worse. “If playtests show rare and deep laws still producing materially higher defence rates than common ones, the answer is more stability cost or a tighter condition, not a smaller number.” Raising a rare law’s stability cost raises the correlation that is the fault.

    And the mechanism it names as the primary reason the split is fair does not discriminate by rank. §7.9 says “every rare and deep law appears in the scout report (12.5)” and charges that visibility against the law’s strength. The scout report is §12.4, not §12.5; what it shows, for 20 Aether a realm and fifteen minutes, is “each realm’s laws” — every rank alike. Visibility cannot be charged against a deep law’s strength when a common law pays the same price for it.

    → Two dials or one, and say which. Either is defensible; what is not is stating the separation and authoring the coupling.

    Keep the separation. Re-cost the sheets so stability cost stops tracking rank — the deep laws are the expensive ones and the change is theirs to absorb — and give rarity its own currency, which §7.6 already has in pages. Then the rare laws have to earn their rank on specificity, and r = −0.04 says they currently do not.

    Or drop it. Rewrite §7.9 to say rank is a strength ladder paid for in pages, which is what the sheets describe and what §7.9’s own counter-evidence [208] says every shipped game does anyway. §7.1’s glossary line goes with it.

    The scout-report paragraph is wrong either way and is drafted below. tools/law_ranks.py runs the measurement and tools/validate_content.py reports it on every build, so whichever way this goes the sheets cannot drift back without saying so.

    v3.3 Decided by withdrawing the claim. §7.9 is now “Rank is a strength ladder, paid for in pages” and says the earlier claim is withdrawn rather than enforced. Its figures check against the sheets: r = +0.79, medians 13.5, 17, 19 and 22.5.

    1 edit to the document
    1. Replace§7.9

      nowA deep law is more dramatic, not more efficient - and every rare and deep law appears in the scout report (12.5). Raiders can see it coming and plan around it. This visibility is charged against the law's strength the way range is charged against a character's kit, and it is the primary reason a rare law can be exciting without being unfair.

      becomesA deep law is more dramatic, not more efficient. Every law in a realm appears in the paid scout (12.4), at 20 Aether per realm and valid for fifteen minutes, so raiders can see one coming and plan around it - but they see a common law coming on the same terms, which means visibility cannot be what pays for a deep law's strength. What pays for it is stability cost, and that is the dial this section separates from rarity.

      §12.5 is Planning; the scout report is §12.4, and it shows every rank alike. The paragraph names this as the primary reason the split is fair, so a mechanism that does not discriminate by rank cannot be left standing as one. D31.

    D25

    No crew in the harness could see §5.4’s clock, so nothing priced in time could be measured at all

    change Done backend
    §5.4§12.19§12.6

    unblocks F20

    Chasing the clock — the dial F15, F16, F18 and F20 all point at — the first experiment was to shorten §5.4’s clock and watch the stopping decision move. It did not move. Cutting the clock to 55% of its published length changed E[grade × fill] by under 4% at every stopping threshold and left the peak exactly where it was.

    That looked like a finding: the clock is not a lever. It was not. No policy in the harness read heist.clock. The crew used the tick counter to rate-limit its own decisions and to time the crack cadence, and never once compared the time left against the walk home. A clock-blind crew not responding to the clock is a fact about the harness, not about Ruleborn.

    §12.19 states the requirement in the sentence the whole break-even rests on — “loading longer earns more and the alarm clock is the price”. A price nobody can see is not a price, and a model where nobody can see it cannot test the claim.

    Caught before publishing, unlike D24, and by the same habit: ask what the model would have to be doing for the result to mean what it appears to mean.

    → Competent and Optimal crews now leave when the time left no longer covers the walk home, estimated the way a player would estimate it — the way out is the way in, so what it cost to reach the Vault is what it will cost to leave, plus 15%. Careless still ignores it, which is what makes it careless.

    The margin is chosen, not derived, and it is the one number here to playtest rather than to trust. It is also biased in a known direction: the way in is crouched and routed around cones, the way out is a run, so estimating the walk home from the inbound time makes crews leave earlier than they need to. That is the conservative direction for everything measured through it.

    The structural guard is a fingerprint. Both of this session’s harness faults were found by reading the model, not by anything going red, because every other test in the suite asserts a band rather than a value — which is right for a finding and useless for a silent change. test_the_harness_gives_the_same_answers_as_when_it_was_last_read hashes the grade, length, fill, decision count and alarm of 40 runs. A deliberate model change updates the digest and says what moved; anything else is a change nobody meant.

    It moves the baseline: mean fill on a successful run falls from 40% to 37% at the published clock, because crews that reached the Vault late now abort instead of loading into a clock they cannot beat — which is correct behaviour and was not being modelled. F14, F18, F19 and F20 were all re-measured through it.

    D57

    The harness ran v3.2’s wards and budgets, and its crews stood still wherever a ward had no way round

    change Done backend re-measured
    §10.3§5.2§10.2§11.1§13.3

    D56 ported v3.3’s rules to sim/ and the harness’s crouch and crack. The harness’s wards were still v3.2’s: every ward fired on its own tile, disarmed in 3 s plus 1 s a level from beside it, reset in 10 s less one a level, and §5.2’s budgets were 3 + realm level wards and 1, 1, 2, 2 and 3 posts. v3.3 gives the Gravity Well a 3-tile sensor and the Lantern Glare a 2-tile one, a 15-second disarm standing on the ward, resets of 10, 12 and 20 s, a measured budget of 8, 8, 6, 7 and 8 wards and 1, 1, 2, 3 and 3 posts, and a 25% assist bonus.

    Porting them exposed two faults in the crews, both older than v3.3. A crew that found no way round a live ward stood in front of it: it recorded “through”, stopped for the tick, and asked again the next, counting a crew decision every other second while it did. A member beside a crossing realm’s link re-planned to another tile beside it, and where the tiles between were covered the nearest was the long way round, so the crew was never beside the link at once. On-tile wards rarely left no way round; a Glare two tiles from a Vault always does, and with v3.3’s sensors every raid on a wards-only realm ran out its clock in the first realm.

    What the fixes moved on v3.2’s wards, same seeds, 180 raids across realms 1, 3 and 5, three realms crossed: held 64.4% → 68.3%, median crew decisions 21 → 19. The decision count moved most where wards are dense: realm 1 on eleven wards went from 33 to 26 decisions (n=200). And what an attempt is worth at realm 3, stopping at 70%, fell from 0.111 to 0.059 (n=300): standing still in front of a ward is also never walking into it, so the old crews were kept out of the Glares they could not go round, by the fault.

    Walking through exposed a third: a crew stopped to crack wherever it first stood beside the Vault, so three members could stand on a Glare there and re-light it at every reset until the clock ran out. A crew that goes round wards now moves to a tile beside the Vault no ward reaches, where there is one.

    → Done. The harness builds v3.3’s wards and budgets by default, reading sensor reach and resets from content/wards.json and the budgets from design_facts, and plays the assist bonus. generate(rules="v3.2") builds the islands every earlier ward and budget number was measured on, and the tests that pin another layer’s finding use it, as they switch the crack noise off for F32 — because v3.3’s Glares decide nearly every raid the generator’s islands hold (F33). The two faults are fixed and pinned. Re-measured after the fixes (crack noise off, v3.2’s wards): F22’s cell 66.0% → 70.0%; F26’s realm 1 at one post and level 5, 42.0% → 43.6%, and two posts 80.0% → 81.2%; realm 3 on six wards 48.0% → 50.5%, on ten 68.0% → 74.5%; designed geometry about three times the generator’s (F16). T0.11’s crew that clears the Heart first is in as well (F32).

    change Open frontend & design
    §12.4§12.12§5.4§9.4§10.3§11.8§23.2§23.5

    §12.4’s scout shows each realm’s laws, the number and roles of its guards, and “how many wards of each type it has, but not where they are”. §12.12: “A scout shows no positions (12.4); patrols are learned in the heist” (C37, settled by brief 38). Each changes what a player can see, which §23.5 builds only once written; §23.5 lists only this screen’s Land here flag.

The document needs some of it. §5.4 makes a landing heard “unless the spot is in fog, darkness or tall grass”, so the raider must see the edge’s terrain, and §23.2’s Landing picker row asks for “Every outer realm’s edge, what guards would hear”, which itself tells where guards stand. §10.3 marks the Crystal Wall and the Thorn Hedge as always seen, and §11.8’s Cartographer sells “a full scouting map of one target, with ward positions”. The design shows the whole realm in 3D with the Vault’s beam and a route to it (realm_diorama.js:255-266). F46 records that every island’s layout is public before any scout, so whatever is hidden is hidden by the client. Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: the scout report shows §12.4’s facts and nothing placed: each realm’s laws, its guards’ number and roles, its wards by type, and one rough loot estimate. The 3D view draws the ground and terrain, the buildings and the Vault, the links and the wards §10.3 marks always seen, and no guard post, patrol or hidden ward unless a Cartographer’s map shows it; the landing picker marks each edge spot covered or open from the terrain alone. One sentence in §12.4 says so, and §23.5 gains the scout row. The alternatives are the design’s scout, or loot by realm as well.

    F24

    v3.1’s supersession check passes on a document that still contains the model it was written to ban

    finding Fixed in the document backend
    §31.5§31.9§7.6§9.5§29.2

    v3.1 bans four superseded models by regular expression and reports all four absent. One of them is not.

    The pattern for the retired three-rank page costs is 15, 30 or 60 pages. §9.5 and §29.2 were both rewritten to the five-rank 10, 20, 35 or 60, so the pattern finds nothing and the check goes green. §7.6 still says it, in different words, in normative text:

    Restoring a law: 15 pages for a common law, 30 for a rare one, 60 for a deep one.

    Same model, same three ranks, same numbers, one clause rearranged — and the check cannot see it. This register’s own check_edits.py found it from the other side: of C23’s four drafted edits, three no longer match the document because the sentences were fixed, and the fourth still matches exactly.

    The general fault is not this regex. It is that a banned-phrasing check can only prove a phrasing absent, never a model, and it reports the stronger claim. §31.5 calls these checks “a string or an arithmetic comparison over the built artefact, so it cannot be argued with” — true, and the thing it cannot be argued with about is narrower than the name on the check.

    → Two changes, and the second is the one that generalises.

    1. Fix §7.6, which is C23’s surviving edit and a one-line replacement.

    2. Derive the ban from the data rather than from a phrase. The page costs live in one place; a check that recomputes every price in the document against that table catches any phrasing, including ones nobody thought of. The same applies to the other three bans: “one 120° cone” does not cover every way to write a single-cone model.

    This is §31.4’s own rule — generated, not authored — pointed at the checks instead of the tables. A hand-written list of forbidden strings is an authored artefact, and it drifts from the thing it describes exactly as C21 to C24 did.

    Two of the four bans are now derived, and the second one closed a blocking item nobody had noticed was closed. The detection model is read out of §12.17’s own two tables rather than searched for: every guard row has a cone, at least two graded zones inside it and a corner-of-the-eye angle wider than the cone — a property a single-cone model cannot be given by rewording — and every guard-state threshold stated anywhere in the prose has to resolve against §12.17’s table, so investigate at 50% fails because 50 is not 600 rather than because of the percent sign. --self-test plants the retired model in other words and prints the ban green beside the derived check red.

    It also reads content/detection.json against the same two tables, which nothing did: the content file was checked for internal consistency and never against the section it was extracted from, which is D30’s fault with the version pointer fixed and the numbers still unchecked.

    All four bans are derived now (D38). The other two followed: retired names read case-insensitively with word boundaries, and every constant read by its unit rather than by the one sentence that defines it, so a second tick rate stated in any other words is compared against §24.10 instead of against nothing. Six restatements of the four defects, in the wording a writer would reach for: the shipped gate catches none, this one catches all six.

    It is tracked to C21 and C1, both closed, so it reports PASS rather than silence — and if either model ever comes back in any wording, a tracked check failing on a closed item breaks the build instead of quietly reopening an argument.

    The page-cost half is built; §7.6 is still yours. tools/check_document.py derives the page costs rather than recognising them: it reads the rank table, reads all 48 sheets, and then checks every rank-to-pages claim in the document in each of the three grammatical forms that carry one — the enumerated “10, 20, 35 or 60 pages by rank”, the arithmetic “18 common × 10 + …”, and the prose form §7.6 uses. It reports §7.6. --self-test plants that sentence in an otherwise clean document and prints both verdicts side by side, so the gap is demonstrated rather than described.

    v3.1’s four phrase bans are kept alongside it, because a verbatim reintroduction is a real way for a deleted model to return and they catch it for nothing. What changed is that they are no longer the only guard on their models. This item stays open because §7.6 still says it — the checking gap is closed, the document fault is not, and those were always two different things.

    F26

    §13.2’s hold band falls inside a gap the defence cannot enter at realm 1

    finding Fixed in the document backend re-measured
    §13.2§19.27§10.2§5.2§12.6§13.3

    waits on F22, F7 · unblocks F27

    §13.2 wants a defence to hold 30 to 45% of raids. §19.27 wants a median run to carry 15 to 25 decisions. The two are set in different sections and never checked against each other, and F7 already showed the second is a statement about depth — 10 decisions across one realm, 17 across two, 24 across three. So the depth is fixed by §19.27 before the hold rate is measured at all.

    Swept across every setting §10.2 and §5.2 permit — one to three guard posts, nought to two geometry bands, Guardian Post levels 1 to 5 — at the depths §12.6’s decision band implies. At realm 1, none of the 24 combinations reaches both bands. Not one.

    At three realms crossed, with the decision count comfortably inside §19.27’s band:

    strongest island on one post  24.2% ± 1.5  3.8 SE below the band
    weakest island on two posts   62.4% ± 1.7  10.1 SE above it     (n=800 a cell)

    A 38-point gap, and §13.2’s band is 15 points wide and sits entirely inside it. The smallest unit of defence the document has is one guard, and at realm 1 that unit is worth two and a half times the width of the band it has to land in. You cannot tune an integer.

    §10.2’s Guardian Post ladder is the one dial finer than a whole guard, and it was built into the harness for this item rather than assumed away. It does not rescue realm 1: its entire range moves the hold rate 15.0% to 20.0% there. What it does elsewhere is F27.

    Realm 2 is the case that can be fixed, and the fix arrives late. One post and two bands holds 21.5% at post level 1 and 31.5% at level 5, inside the band. But §10.2 prices a level-3 post at 4,060 Starlight and its own column says an engaged player builds one on day 36, while §5.2 opens realm 2 at Keeper 6 and §14.2 puts an engaged player there on day 5. Thirty-one days defending a realm that cannot reach the band the document sets for it, and longer for everyone slower: day 8 for a regular player, day 16 for a casual one.

    Why it bites at realm 1 and not above. §5.2 gives posts by 1 + (level−1)÷2, so the smallest increment available to the guard layer is a share of what is already there: +100% at realms 1 and 2, +50% at realms 3 and 4. Measured, that is what the jump looks like — adding the second post at realm 1 is worth +45.7 points of hold rate, while adding the third at realm 3 is worth +12.5. Part of the difference is the ceiling rather than the step, since realm 3 is already at 85% before the third post, so this is offered as the shape of the mechanism and not as a clean decomposition.

    One thing that is not the mechanism, recorded because this item asserted it first. An earlier draft observed that §5.2 grows the grid every level while the post count does not, so coverage sawtooths — 100 tiles a guard at realm 1, 121 at realm 2, 72 at realm 3 — and said defence per tile therefore falls on the level a player has just reached. The arithmetic is right and it predicts nothing. With posts forced to one at every realm, so coverage falls monotonically from 100 to 196 tiles a guard, the hold rate rises monotonically:

    realm  tiles/guard  wards    hold
      1      100      4   19.2% ± 2.0
      3      144      6   26.2% ± 2.2
      5      196      8   55.5% ± 2.5

    Wards and route length dominate guard coverage, so tiles per guard is a real number about §5.2 and not a lever on §13.2.

    Scope. All of this is measured on generated islands, which is the population §13.3 made the default and F16 measured at a fraction of a designed one. A designer can place geometry at a resolution the post count does not have — that is F16’s finding — so this is about the islands most players will defend and raid, not about what the editor can build.

    Re-measured after D55, in part (generator sweep, same seeds and sample sizes): 3 of 10 realm/depth combinations have a setting inside both bands, as before, and the nearest misses are the same cells within a few points. The ward budget agrees on both harnesses: the recorded ward needs for realms 2–5 are confirmed. For realm 1 the recorded 10 did not land both bands on the D55 harness — 11 did — but with F31’s split on top it lands again: on the current harness every recorded need, realm 1’s 10 included, is confirmed.

    → The lever is wards, and §5.2 allows 40% of what is needed. An earlier draft of this recommendation said realm 1 had no lever at the right scale, and listed wards, grid size and a relaxed band as untested candidates. Wards are now tested and they are the answer.

    Realm 1, three realms crossed, one guard post, one geometry band, n=800 a cell:

    wards   hold        decisions
       4   19.2% ± 2.0   20  §5.2’s own limit
       8   27.6% ± 1.6   22
      10   30.8% ± 1.6   24  inside both bands
      12   41.1% ± 1.7   26  one decision over

    §5.2 gives realm 1 four wards (3 + realm level) and it takes ten. The ward axis has the resolution the post count lacks — each ward is worth two to four points where a guard is worth forty-six — so the band is reachable there and nowhere else. The window is narrow: ten wards sits just inside the bottom of the hold band, and twelve is comfortably inside it but one decision past §19.27’s ceiling.

    Wards are not orthogonal to the decision count, which F22 assumed of the two knobs it swept: every ward adds decisions as well as hold, so both bands are spent from one budget. That is why nothing works at two geometry bands — seven wards reaches 33.4% and carries 26 decisions — and why the answer is one band with more wards rather than the reverse.

    The post count is still not a candidate, and neither is the post ladder (F27).

    And the fix is per realm, because a flat ward count fails the same collateral check the post ladder did. Ten wards everywhere rescues realm 1 and loses both bands at realms 3 and 5 — 34.4% to 53.6% and 39.8% to 47.2% — while sending realm 2 to 65.8%. Measured per realm at each one’s best settings, n=500 a cell:

    realm  §5.2 gives  needs    hold       dec
      1        4      10   30.4% ± 2.1  24
      2        5       8   37.6% ± 2.2  21
      3        6       6   34.4% ± 2.1  23  correct
      4        7       7   40.4% ± 2.2  17  correct
      5        8       8   39.8% ± 2.2  18  correct

    Every realm can satisfy both bands, and §5.2’s formula is right from realm 3 up and wrong below. 3 + realm level gives 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; what is needed is 11, 8, 6, 7, 8 — ten at realm 1 in this table, eleven when the sweep is run as a whole, below. The formula increases with realm level and the need does not — realm 1 needs more wards than any other realm, and gets the fewest.

    That is not a paradox once the raider is looked at: the crew does not scale with realm level, so a low realm starts from further behind and needs more compensation, not less. Measured directly — posts forced to one at every realm — the hold rate rises from 19.2% at realm 1 to 55.5% at realm 5 on the same crew. §5.2 scales the defence with the realm when it should be scaling it against the raider.

    Realm 1 is the one narrow window: ten wards sits at the bottom edge of the hold band and twelve is one decision past §19.27’s ceiling, so ten or eleven is the whole of it.

    Fix realm 2’s window. The fix exists and arrives 31 days after the realm does. Front-load the post ladder, open realm 2 later, or start a realm’s first post above level 1 — the last is closest to §13.3’s own promise that a generated defence is “never empty”, which is currently a claim about contents rather than about strength.

    This is not F22 restated. F22 found the band unreachable at §5.2’s one post and recommended a floor of two; measured at the depth §19.27’s decision band actually implies, two posts overshoot. The floor F22 asks for is the right direction and it does not land in the band either. Both items are the same quantisation seen from opposite sides.

    Run as a table rather than a column, the budget is 11, 8, 6, 7, 8. Everything above was measured one realm at a time. tools/ward_budget.py sweeps the ward count and the geometry band count at every realm and reports what each one needs; four of the five rows come back confirmed and realm 1 moves by one ward. At one band, n=400: ten wards holds 29.5% ± 2.3 with 24 decisions — half a point under §13.2’s floor — and eleven holds 32.5% ± 2.3 with 25. This item already said “ten or eleven is the whole of it”; measured at four times the sample it is eleven, and the window is one ward wide.

    Every realm is reachable, and none of them at nought geometry bands. Across 150 settings — five realms, three band counts, ten ward counts — every setting that satisfies both bands has one band or two, and at nought the ward count barely moves the defence at all: realm 1 runs 4.0% at three wards to 13.0% at twelve. A ward is worth almost nothing without geometry to hide it behind, which §13.4’s independent per-layer budget has no way to say — it prices the layers separately and one of them is conditional on another.

    The window widens with realm level, which is the same fact as the budget running the other way to §5.2’s formula: realm 1 has one setting in 30, realm 2 has two, realm 4 has nine. The realms the formula gives fewest wards are the realms with least room to be wrong.

    python3 -m tools.generator_settings · python3 -m tools.ward_budget

    v3.3 Decided. The ward limit is eight at most, set per level by the hold band (8, 8, 6, 7, 8), and generated islands at realm level 1 get their own band, 25 to 40%, by a stated rule. The holds are measured before the peripheral-vision alignment, and realm level 4 at two posts rather than three; §13.2 says both and defers them to the re-run.

    F22

    §5.2’s one guard post puts §13.2’s band out of reach at realms 1 and 2, whatever the generator does

    finding Fixed in the document backend re-measured
    §5.2§13.2§13.3§12.22§13.4

    waits on C5, Q8 · unblocks F11, F26, F9

    Found while building the generator F16 argued for, which is the useful part: the fix worked and then stopped short of the band, and the reason it stopped is not the generator.

    §5.2 gives a realm 1 + (level − 1) // 2 guard posts, so realms 1 and 2 get one. Competent crew, sign-aware laws, two realms crossed, 400 raids a cell:

    realm 1, 1 post   0 bands  5.5%  1 band 12.0%  2 bands 16.5%
    realm 1, 2 posts  0 bands 15.5%  1 band 44.8%  2 bands 51.5%
    realm 2, 1 post   0 bands 13.0%  1 band 17.5%  2 bands 21.5%
    realm 2, 2 posts  0 bands 30.2%  1 band 56.8%  2 bands 68.8%

    At one post the band is unreachable. Realm 1 tops out at 16.5% and realm 2 at 21.5%, against a band that starts at 30%. Geometry is worth 11 points at realm 1; the gap to the band is 14 points after geometry has done everything it can. The second post is worth 35 points — more than every other lever combined.

    The mechanism is F15’s, and this is the second finding to land on it: guards are half of the island’s only detect-and-act chain. Geometry, wards and laws work by delay, and delay reaches an outcome only through §5.4’s clock, which has four times the slack any delay needs. One guard is almost no detection, so there is very little for the delay to convert into.

    Realms 1 and 2 are where every new player starts, and F13 is this seen from the matchmaker: §12.22 promises a median target in a 55–70% raider-success band, and this pool runs at 78–95%.

    One thing checked before it was claimed. The gain from geometry looks larger when a second post is present — +7 points at one post against +29 at two — which reads as the two layers multiplying. They do not. On the log-odds scale, which is the scale a bounded probability adds on, the interaction is +0.05 ± 0.32 (t = 0.15): geometry and guards are independent, and the apparent synergy is the percentage scale compressing near zero. Unlike guards and response (F15), which really are multiplicative, §13.2’s separable shares are the right model here.

    Re-measured after D55 (generator sweep, same seeds and sample sizes): at one post realm 1 still peaks at 16.7% (was 15.0%) and realm 2 at 29.8% (was 26.2%), under §13.2’s 30% floor. Realm 1 with two posts and one band moved from 44.8% to 48.8%, now just over the band rather than inside it. The finding holds: one post cannot reach the band. With F31’s split on top it still holds — realm 1 peaks at 19.5%, realm 2 at 28.5%.

    → Specified in docs/design/spec/generator.md. A floor of two posts at realms 1 and 2 — one line, and the only change measured that brings those realms within reach at all. The line is in §10.2, not §5.2 as this item first said: §5.2 carries no post count at all, and the rule lives in §10.2’s Guardian Post entry — “Every realm; 1 to 3 by realm level”. Recorded rather than quietly corrected, because a recommendation that names the wrong section is the same fault as a citation that does, and this one survived until the edit was drafted against the document.

    Two further things fall out of the same grid.

    The knobs are nearly orthogonal, which is the specification §13.3 is missing. Bands drive the decision count (6 → 13 → 15 at realm 1) and barely touch the hold rate’s driver; posts drive the hold rate and move decisions by 0 to 2. So: lay bands until §19.27’s 15–25 decisions is met, then fill posts until §13.2’s 30–45% is met, in that order.

    The geometry has to be a dial, not a switch. On or off, realm 1 at two posts gives 15.5% or 51.5% and steps straight over the band; one band lands at 44.8%. A realm has very few discrete settings early — integer posts, 3 + level wards — and a layer offered as a switch cannot be balanced against a 15-point band.

The cell F22 was first measured in — two posts, two realms — reads 66.0%, against 44.8% under v3.2's rules; generator_settings --self-test pins the new value.

    After D57's fixes, on v3.2's wards: one post at level 5 43.6% and two posts 81.2% (70.4% and 92.8% with the noise), and F22's cell 70.0%.

    F10

    Sixteen of forty-eight laws are parameter changes; the rest need an engine feature

    finding Fixed in the document backend
    §7.3§12.21§24§26.1

    waits on C26 · unblocks D6, G10, Q5

    §7.3 is the architectural claim the whole design rests on — laws change a realm’s rule sheet rather than containing special cases — and v3.0’s §12.21 turns it into a rule: “every tier effect of every law must be expressible as a change to a named parameter”. Written out for all 48 laws against a rule sheet of twenty named parameters:

    parameter 16   authored 4   attribute 2   entity 10   event 16

    Sixteen are parameter changes and nothing else. Ten need the simulation to spawn and track an object it otherwise has no reason to know about — braziers, puffballs, afterimages, illusory guards. Sixteen need a periodic or conditional rule: Rewind restores world state from ten seconds ago, which §24.10’s input-log model keeps no snapshots for; Held breath advances time only while a crew member moves, which is not a parameter of the simulation but a different simulation.

    This is not an argument against those laws. It is the engine budget §26.1 does not contain: 32 of them are features, and they were costed as content.

    → Two things follow. Tag every law with its kind before authoring resumes — python3 tools/law_effects.py --write emits the table — so a scope cut can drop the expensive ones rather than the unpopular ones; D6’s proposed cut from 48 laws to 24 is a very different saving depending which 24. And state the rule sheet. §7.3 asserts laws are parameters without ever listing the parameters, and a vocabulary that grows to fit each new law is not a vocabulary.

    Both drafted, in docs/design/spec/laws.md: the twenty parameters are listed, and tools/scope_cut.py costs the cut this finding said would depend on which 24. It does. Weighting each kind by the engine work it needs, all 48 cost 84 points; a cost-aware 24 costs 15 and a 24 chosen by rank costs 39. Choosing which 24 by cost rather than by rank saves 62% of the cut’s remaining engine work for exactly the same amount of content, keeps all sixteen free laws, and still fills §7.7’s six schools evenly at four each.

    The rank split is where the cost hides: of 18 Commons 9 are pure parameter changes, and of 12 Deep laws one is. Depth is bought with engine work — a reasonable design, and an unbudgeted one.

    v3.3 Every sheet in §7.7 now carries an Effect kind tag, and §7.10 is the ladder they sit on: 16 parameter, 6 placement or attribute, 16 conditional, 10 spawned, none on the rewind rung. Tidemark replaces Rewind as a checkpoint return. The extraction keeps the tag as data (content/laws.json: engine_rung, launch).

    v3.0 then added fill to the same formula — “the share of the crew’s bags actually loaded” — and left 0.46 alone. This is C19’s pattern applied to the single number §9.6 names as the one the curve rests on.
