    F21

    Outcomes polarise with skill: the better a crew plays, the more it sweeps or comes home empty

    finding Fixed in the document backend re-measured
    §13.2§12.17§12.19

    waits on F20 · unblocks F19

    §13.2 is unusually explicit about the health signal, and it is not the average: “A game where raids either sweep or fail completely, with nothing in between, is a polarised one even if the mean looks right… We watch the spread of clean runs, partial hauls and foiled raids, and treat a populated middle as the goal.”

    Fill on every successful raid, 300 raids a crew, same islands and seeds — the only difference is how well the crew plays:

                  competent    optimal
      0–19%      30.0%     58.0%
     20–39%      16.5%      0.6%
     40–59%      23.5%      2.4%
     60–79%      30.0%     13.0%
    80–100%       0.0%     26.0%

    middle (20–79%)  70.0%    16.0%

    A competent crew has exactly the populated middle §13.2 asks for. A crew that reads §12.17’s guards has 16% in the middle: it sweeps on a quarter of its successful raids and comes home with almost nothing on more than half.

    The mechanism is the information, not the greed. Reading a guard’s suspicion turns every raid into an early yes-or-no: commit and take everything, or abandon at 35% and walk. There is no reason left to take a middling haul once you can tell which run you are in.

    So §13.2’s warning is tripped, and it is tripped specifically for the players who read the game best — the ones most likely to be visible, to post replays and to set what everyone else copies.

    Re-measured after D55 (the harness now reads peripheral vision as the content file does; same seeds and sample sizes): measured with test_skill_polarises_outcomes’s setup (realm 3, one link, sign-aware laws, 300 raids), which does not reproduce the 30.0% and 58.0% above exactly. On it the polarisation holds on both harnesses: successful raids filling 20–79% are 74% → 70% of a competent crew’s and 9% → 9% of an optimal one’s.

    → This is §13.2’s own health metric failing on its own terms, and the population it fails for is the worst one to fail for. It is also not fixable by tuning the break-even: F20 moves the threshold and the polarisation moves with it.

    What would populate the middle is a reason to leave at a fill the crew did not choose in advance:

    1. The Spire’s reach (spec/response.md) — a Vault that re-seals while it is being robbed sets the fill from outside the crew’s rule entirely.

    2. A flatter Carry spread (§11.1) — the Carrier is 300 of a crew’s 560, so “the Carrier filled” is very nearly the whole distribution. Five similar bags turn one binary into five small decisions.

    3. Make abandoning cost something. Leaving at 35% currently counts as a success and pays almost nothing, which is why it is free to do it often. §12.9’s grades have no band between “partial” and nothing.

    python3 -m tools.heist_harness depth.

    v3.2 Closed with a measurement and a reframing. §13.2: “the health signal is the shape of the outcomes, not the average”, and a polarised game is named as the failure. Measured over 300 raids on identical seeds, a crew following a fixed stopping threshold puts 70% of its runs in one bucket — which is the finding, stated as a property of the design rather than a defect in it.

    F15

    Guards and Response are not two layers; they are one, and three more have no path to the metric

    finding Fixed in the document backend re-measured
    §13.2§13.4§5.4§9.6

    waits on F16, F8, C5 · unblocks F20

    §13.2 lists five defence layers with target shares and one rule above them: no single layer above 25%, because “if one layer decides outcomes, the other four are decoration”. §13.4 specifies exactly how to check it — all 32 combinations, credit divided “the way cooperative game theory does”, which is the Shapley value. At 120 raids a combination:

    geometry  4.4%  (target 25%)
    guards   34.5%  (target 20%)
    wards    20.9%  (target 20%)
    laws     5.7%  (target 20%)
    response  34.5%  (target 15%)

    Guards and Response are equal to the decimal, and that is a theorem rather than a coincidence: in every one of the eight coalitions, guards without response turn back 0% of raids and response without guards turns back 0%. Symmetric players must take identical shares.

    The cause is not that Response lacks an effect of its own. That was this item’s first recommendation; it was specified, built and measured, and it failed — see docs/design/spec/response.md. The real cause is that guards-and-response is the island’s only detect-and-act chain. Geometry, wards and laws all work by delay, and delay reaches an outcome only through the clock — which has four times the slack any delay would need, since a run ends at about 40 seconds of §5.4’s 165. So the island has exactly one way to turn back a raid, it needs both halves, and §13.4’s metric can see nothing else.

    The metric is half the fault. §13.4 measures the hold rate. §12.9 grades a raid clean, loud, partial or foiled and §9.6 pays 1.0, 0.7, 0.4 and 0 — so a defence that turns every clean run into a partial one takes 60% of the raider’s income and scores zero. Re-measured against grade × fill, the identity breaks (guards 38.7%, response 35.4%) and the 69% does not: together they deny 74% of the haul, and geometry and laws get worse, at 1.6% and 3.5%.

    Re-measured after D55 (the harness now reads peripheral vision as the content file does; same seeds and sample sizes): Guards and Response still measure identically — 32.5% each by hold rate (was 30.9%), 40.7% and 35.5% by haul (was 39.6% and 35.3%) — and both stay over §13.2’s 25% ceiling. The generated defence holds 42.5% (was 47.5%), inside the band at 120 raids a coalition. The finding holds.

    → Three changes, in order, specified in docs/design/spec/response.md.

    1. §13.4: measure against what §9.6 pays, not the hold rate. One sentence, and it is the difference between a measurement that can see four of the five layers and one that cannot. It is strictly more information — the hold rate is the special case where grade × fill is zero.

    2. §5.4: the clock is why three layers are decoration. Either tighten it until delay converts to outcomes — which is also what §19.27’s “a quarter of runs decided in the last ten seconds” asks for and does not get — or accept that geometry, wards and laws shape the haul rather than the outcome, and rewrite §13.2’s shares to say which layers do which.

    3. §13.2: specify the Spire’s reach and the guardian Sage’s power — both are named there and neither is defined, and a layer whose two named components have no rules is not a layer. But stop claiming Response is independent of Guards. “Detection and response, 35%” is a layer; “Guards 20%, Response 15%” is one layer counted twice, and that is what breaks the ceiling on paper as well as in the harness.

    Settled by measurement, not by argument. The Spire’s reach and the Sage’s power are now specified and built (spec/response.md), and they work: separately they cost a raider 6% and 18% of the haul with no guard involved. Run through §13.4’s 32 coalitions they still change nothing — guards 39.0% → 39.1%, response 34.7% → 35.1%, and response alone against a bare island stays at 0.0%. Both effects need the crew to have been slowed by something else first: on an undefended island there is nothing for a re-seal to race and nothing for a slow to eat into. The layer is a complement by construction, and specifying it does not change that — so the ceiling breach is a fact about §13.2’s table rather than about the layer’s contents, and change 3 is the operative one.

    python3 -m tools.heist_harness ablation 120 and python3 -m tools.heist_harness haul 120.

    Re-measured on the current harness, and against the generator F16 asked for (80 raids a coalition, realm 3):

                plain  shaped  target
    geometry   8.5%  16.0%   25%
    guards    31.5%   28.8%   20%
    wards     22.5%   18.2%   20%
    laws      6.1%    8.2%   20%
    response  31.5%   28.8%   15%

    Three things, and the first is the one that matters.

    Guards and response are identical to the decimal under both generators. 31.5/31.5 and 28.8/28.8. The symmetry is a theorem about the coalitions, not an artefact of the island it was first measured on, and changing the island wholesale does not disturb it by a tenth of a point.

    Geometry’s share nearly doubles — 8.5% to 16.0% on the hold rate, 0.4% to 7.7% on the haul — which is F16’s claim measured through §13.4’s own method. A good part of what this item recorded as a fact about the layer was a fact about the generator.

    The ceiling breach shrinks and does not close. Guards and response fall from 34.5% to 28.8%, still over §13.2’s 25%, and geometry rises to 16% against its 25% target. So this item’s conclusion stands — the breach is about §13.2’s table — with one correction: it is partly about the generator, and the earlier 4.4% understated the layer.

    v3.3 Changed rather than tuned. Detection and response are one layer at 35%, the 25% ceiling became a rule that no layer decides an outcome alone, and §13.4 measures haul denied across all 16 combinations of four layers. Geometry at 25% and laws at 20% remain targets for the measurement ledger (§32).

    F17

    Aether and Essence have no sinks, because every price in §9.5 is on the wrong kind of curve

    finding Fixed in the document backend
    §9.5§9.3§9.1§10.2§11.6

    unblocks C18, C28

    §9.1 runs the game on three resources and §9.5 prices every sink for all three. A total understates the problem, because a faucet runs every day and almost every price in §9.5 is paid once. Totalled over a whole account to day 301:

    Aether   produced 14,674,532  every price there is 2,968,032  faucet is  5x the sink
    Essence  produced  6,660,571  every price there is   658,501  faucet is 10x the sink

    And that is the best case: at day 301 every Essence price is finished — the roster is capped, every character is level 10 — while the Gardens keep running.

    The cause is not the size of the prices but their shape. From day 2 to day 301 the faucets multiply by 122, 240 and 251. The prices aimed at them multiply by:

    Starlight  a Star Well level     x1,478   faucet x122  → outruns it 12x
    Aether     weaving, upkeep, the Lab      x10   faucet x240  → behind it 24x
    Essence    the next birth           x88   faucet x251  → behind it 3x

    Starlight is permanently scarce because §10.2’s building curve is geometric and never ends. Nothing points a geometric curve at the other two: every price aimed at them is flat (scouting), linear (the Lab, waking) or capped (births at 38, levels at 10), and a bounded price against an unbounded faucet loses by however long the game runs.

    §9.5 has exactly one recurring price and the roster cap makes it unreachable. §11.6 rests a crew 45 minutes and §9.5 charges 2 Essence a level a minute to wake them early — the only price a player pays again every session. It falls due only when nobody rested is left to send, which at the roster cap of 38 is 199 heists a day. §14.2’s engaged player raids four times. Same shape as C19 and F1: §11.5 set the cap, §11.6 set the rest window, nobody divided one by the other.

    Design findings — these change how the game plays

    Not clerical. Each is arithmetic from the document's own published tables, and each asks a question about the design rather than the prose.

    F1

    The roster cannot staff the universe the rules permit

    finding Fixed in the document backend
    §5.2§10.2§11.5§9.3§4

    Pure arithmetic from three published tables. A finished universe has 152 character positions — 126 producer worker slots (7 realms × 2 of each producer × 3 kinds × 3 slots), 21 guard posts, a crew of five — against a roster ceiling of 38 (3 at the Spire plus 7 Hearths × 5 homes). That is 25% coverage; the roster would need to be four times larger. Even production alone at one producer per realm needs 63 workers, before a single guard is posted.

    → This may be intentional — §4 names characters' time as one of two scarce resources. But three things follow that the document has not absorbed: §9.3's production figures are unstaffable; 25% coverage reads as “most of my buildings are idle” rather than as interesting scarcity; and the marginal Star Well becomes worthless, which removes a large part of §10.2's Starlight sink. Decide which lever moves: more Hearth homes, fewer permitted producers, or partial staffing made genuinely worthwhile.

    v3.0 §5.8 decides it: one producer of each kind per realm, partial staffing paying pro-rata, and “the roster can never fill everything — 38 ruleborn against far more positions — and that is the scarcity the design is built on”. Scarcity is now a feature by decision rather than by accident.

    F2

    Building the second producer doubles income and breaks every pacing date

    finding Fixed in the document backend
    §9.3§5.2§14.2§14.3

    Solving backwards from §9.3's day-301 figure implies about seven fully staffed Star Wells at level 9 — one per realm, not the fourteen §5.2 allows. Running the economy model under all four readings, only “one producer per realm, no binding roster cap” tracks the document (117% of published at day 301; Keeper 40 on day 171 against a published 181). Every other reading is out by 2–4×.

    finding Fixed in the document both
    §13.3§7.7§5.5

    F27

    §10.2’s post ladder is the right size and starts in the wrong place, so the same upgrade is required, free or harmful

    finding Fixed in the document backend re-measured
    §10.2§13.2§5.2

    waits on F26

    Split out of F26, which measured the ladder while answering a different question and then had to keep amending itself.

    §10.2 sells Guardian Posts at five levels, “+10% health and sight” each. Measured at that slope, what buying a post from level 1 to level 5 does, by realm:

    realm  level 1  level 5  span
      1    15.0%   24.2%   9.2  entirely below the band
      2    26.2%   38.8%  12.6  enters it only at the top
      3    34.2%   44.4%  10.2  inside throughout
      4    40.0%   52.7%  12.7  leaves it at the top
      5    40.0%   55.3%  15.3  leaves it at the top     (n=1,200 at realms 3 to 5)

    The ladder spans 12 points on average against a band 15 points wide — almost exactly the right size to be the tuning dial §13.2 needs. What is wrong is where each realm’s ladder begins, and §5.2’s post formula sets that. Of five realms it lands one inside the band.

    So the same purchase does three different things depending where it is made: at realm 2 it is required to reach the band, at realm 3 it is free, and at realms 4 and 5 it carries the defence out of the band — 52.7% and 55.3%, 5.3 and 7.2 standard errors past 45%. Nothing in §10.2 says so, and a player buying an upgrade is not told they are leaving the design’s own health band.

    Realm 3 read as over at 400 raids and is inside at 1,200 — 44.4% ± 1.4. Recorded because it is the fourth time in this register that a number near a boundary moved once the sample was earned, and the claim it would have supported — that the ladder takes every upper realm out of the band — is wider than the evidence carries.

    Re-measured after D55 (the harness now reads peripheral vision as the content file does; same seeds and sample sizes): one number changed and the verdict did not. Realm 1 needs twice §10.2’s slope to reach the band (20% a level: 33.2%), not five times — the corner of the eye now carries more of what sight buys, so a sight upgrade buys more. At that slope a maxed post still carries all four upper realms out of the top: 52.2%, 58.2%, 64.0%, 62.0%. So the ladder still does not close the gap; it moves it up the realm levels, at a smaller slope than recorded.

    → Fix the base, not the dial. State a starting defence per realm chosen so the ladder spans the band — realm 2 higher, realms 4 and 5 lower — rather than letting it fall out of 1 + (level−1)÷2. The ladder itself is the right instrument and needs no change.

    A steeper ladder is not the answer, and was measured rather than reasoned about. F26 first recommended doubling its effect to rescue realm 1, and since D55 doubling does reach the band there — 20% a level holds 33.2% (before D55 it took five times §10.2’s slope). But at that slope a maxed post carries all four upper realms out of the top — 52.2%, 58.2%, 64.0%, 62.0%. The ladder does not close realm 1’s gap; it moves it up the realm levels. One slope has to serve every realm, and the realms that work sit near the top of the band already, so any upgrade large enough to matter at realm 1 carries them out of it. Withdrawn with the numbers, on the same principle as F17’s and F20’s withdrawn edits.

    Say what an upgrade is for. If §13.2’s band is the health metric, §10.2 currently sells four realms an upgrade that leaves it. Either the band is not meant to hold for an upgraded island — in which case say so — or the base moves.

    python3 -m tools.post_ladder

    v3.3 The Guardian Post ladder keeps one slope and sets its start per realm level, so each level’s midpoint sits in its band. The starts for realm levels 1 and 2 are computed until the aligned re-run.

    F20

    The best fixed stopping rule is about 90% full, not §12.19’s 70%

    finding Fixed in the document backend re-measured
    §12.19§9.6§5.4§12.17

    waits on D25, F15 · unblocks F21

    §12.19 makes the most falsifiable claim in the document and says it is load-bearing: “The break-even sits at about 70% full — at that point the extra load is worth exactly what a loud exit costs. That single number is the dial for the game’s emotional peak.”

    §9.6 says what a raid is worth, and a stopping rule moves two of its terms, so the quantity to maximise is E[grade × fill]. Hold everything else about a competent crew fixed and vary only where it stops. 300 raids a row:

    stops at  50%  E = 0.1022 ± 0.0089
    stops at  60%  E = 0.1113 ± 0.0103
    stops at  70%  E = 0.1271 ± 0.0116  ← 12.19’s
    stops at  80%  E = 0.1315 ± 0.0128
    stops at  90%  E = 0.1646 ± 0.0157  ← peak
    stops at 100%  E = 0.1589 ± 0.0161

    Loading past 70% is worth about 30% more an attempt and costs nothing measurable in success rate (56.7% at 70%, 54.7% at 90%). A break-even exists, as §12.19 says; it sits about twenty points above where §12.19 puts it, which makes the region the document calls the decision a slope.

    And no fixed rule is the best rule. A crew that reads §12.17’s visible suspicion and varies its threshold gets 0.187, beating the best fixed threshold by 13% (F19). The decision §12.6 asks for is real — it is just not the decision §12.19 describes.

    Settled at §13.4’s own sample size. The sweeps above read a peak off an argmax, which is a noisy statistic; paired over the same seeds at 700 raids a threshold the comparison is decisive:

    stops at  70%  E = 0.1231  success 53.3%
    stops at  80%  E = 0.1370  +0.0139 ± 0.0077  t = 1.8
    stops at  90%  E = 0.1595  +0.0364 ± 0.0080  t = 4.5  success 52.0%

    +30% an attempt for 1.3 points of success rate. That matters because at the sweeps’ own sample sizes the same comparison is only t ≈ 2.3, and it had been run several times — marginal evidence, repeated, which is how the two findings withdrawn beside this one happened. It is not marginal at 700.

    Measured twice more than it should have needed besides: at 150 raids a row the curve rose all the way to 100%, which would have meant no break-even at all, and that did not survive a larger sample; the numbers above are after D25.

    Re-measured after D55 (the harness now reads peripheral vision as the content file does; same seeds and sample sizes): the best fixed stopping point is still 95% (E 0.1760 → 0.1805), and stopping at 70% still costs about a third: +37% at the peak against +33%. The finding holds.

    → Specified in docs/design/spec/loading.md.

    1. Re-derive the number rather than asserting it. python3 -m tools.heist_harness breakeven prints the curve and the break-even is where it turns over. 70% is not where it turns over.

    2. Say that the rule should vary. §12.19 describes a single threshold; the measurement says a crew reading the guards beats every single threshold. That is the decision §12.6 wants and §12.17 already provides the information for, and the document does not connect them.

    3. Give staying a price that is not the clock. §12.19 names one — “the alarm clock is the price” — and cutting §5.4’s clock to 55% of its length moves the stopping decision not at all: a tighter clock kills crews on the way in. A cost priced in loot does bite where a cost priced in time does not, which is the best argument for the Spire’s reach in spec/response.md.

    Measured, and it works. With the Spire’s reach re-sealing 8 units a second the peak moves from 100% to 90%; at 15 a second it moves to 60%. The rate is a dial on where the raider’s break-even sits, and §12.19’s stated 70% falls between the two — so the document’s number is not wrong, it is unimplemented. §12.19 describes the game as it would be with a mechanism §13.2 names and never specifies.

    The cost, and the rule in §9.6 that removes it: raising the rate raises the hold rate too (45.0% → 48.5% → 53.0%) against §13.2’s 30–45% band, because a fast re-seal empties the Vault before a slow crew loads anything and the raid is foiled. §9.6 already forbids that outcome — “a clean raid on a fully sealed island still pays 0.7; nobody ever leaves with nothing”. With that floor applied to the re-seal, 20 a second stopping at 45% moves the break-even from 100% to 80% and leaves the hold rate at 44.5%, inside the band and within noise of the 45.0% baseline.

    So two things the document names and never specifies — §13.2’s “the Spire’s reach” and §9.6’s floor — combine to make §12.19’s sentence very nearly true. The number was not wrong; the mechanism that would have justified it was missing.

    v3.2 Closed. §12.19 now states “the curve peaks at about 90% full and turns over after it”, measured over 300 raids with only the stopping point varying. §32.1 adds why the old figure was wrong in a way worth keeping: 70% is close to the threshold the one peer-reviewed study of this exact decision names as the rule first-time players intuitively choose, and trained agents beat it.

      nowThe break-even sits at about 70% full — at that point the extra load is worth exactly what a loud exit costs.

      becomesThe break-even sits at about 70% full once the Spire’s reach is re-sealing the Vault as the crew loads (13.2); with nothing re-sealing it, the best fixed rule is nearer 90%.

      Measured over 700 paired raids a threshold, stopping at 90% beats §12.19’s 70% by +0.0364 ± 0.0080 an attempt (t = 4.5) for 1.3 points of success rate. So the number is not wrong — it is unimplemented: it describes the game as it would be with a mechanism §13.2 names and never specifies. At a re-seal of 20 a second with §9.6’s own floor applied, the peak moves to 80% and the hold rate stays at 44.5%, inside the band.

    Regrowth     health_regen 2%/s   buildings, wards and guards
    Thorns       health_drain 5%     per touch of a wall or hedge

    The Friends screen must show a “co-op lobby”. §26.1 puts co-op heists under after launch. §12.11 says “Co-op heists (version 1.1)” and §27.2 says “friendly heists, sharing and the Island Workshop at launch; co-op heists in version 1.1”. The other three appear nowhere in it, which is the evidence that §23.2 is a launch list and this row is the exception rather than the rule.

    And a lobby is the wrong object anyway. §30.8’s decision table rejects “real-time co-op as scoped” — “full netcode cost for a mode outside the core loop” — and decides “asynchronous co-op first; real-time only if playtests demand it”. §12.11 carries that: “asynchronous first: the first version is turn-based”. A lobby is where players gather at the same moment. An asynchronous turn-based mode has an invitation and a queue, and no lobby at all. The screen list still carries a control from the design the review threw out.

    §23.2 was updated for §30.8’s other interface-visible decisions, which is what makes this one a miss rather than an oversight of the whole table: free chat for minors became “chat (preset for 13 to 15)”, teaching the 44 resonances became “discovered resonances”, and virtual-currency obfuscation became “Sets with real prices”. Three of four followed. This is the fourth.

    → Two words. The Friends row becomes “Friends’ feed, friendly heists, invitations, gifts”, and the co-op screen is listed under 1.1 with the rest of the mode — as an invitation and turn queue, not a lobby, so the screen the designer eventually draws matches the mode that will exist. Drafted below.

    The other 128 items are specified, and two of them nearly were not. A scan for must-show terms the document never uses elsewhere reported six gaps. Reading them found four were the scan’s fault, and two are worth recording because they are F24’s lesson in the mirror. §23.2’s Scout report must show matchups, a word that appears nowhere else — but §11.5 specifies it under another name: “each resists exactly one law family, so crew choice against a scouted island is a real decision (12.4)”, and ruleborn.json carries a resists field for all eighteen. Spotlights read as absent because the scan looked for the plural; §18.6 specifies it.

    F24 is that a banned phrase can prove a phrasing absent, never a model. The mirror image is that a missing phrase proves a phrasing absent, never a gap, and it is the more dangerous of the two, because a false gap sends someone to design something that already exists. Both faults were caught by reading the hits rather than counting them, which is the only method that works on either.

    v3.3 Co-op is asynchronous and turn-based, in version 1.1, with no lobby (§12.11, §23.2).

    §9.6§12.19§12.17§14.2

    §9.6: Haul = B(V) × grade × difficulty × richness × fatigue × fill, and it calls 0.46 — E[grade] over all attempts — “the number the progression curve is built on”. Two of those terms move with how a raid is played, so the quantity to measure is E[grade × fill] per attempt. Same islands, same seeds, 300 raids each:

    stops at 12.19’s break-even   E = 0.127 an attempt
    reads the guards, then decides  E = 0.187 an attempt

    1.47×, and both are far below §9.6’s 0.46 — which is E[grade] alone and takes no account of the fill term v3.0 added beside it (F14).

It uses what §12.17 already shows the player — a guard’s suspicion and the path of its cone — to push to 95% when nothing has noticed and leave at 35% when something has.     That distinction is the reason this finding was briefly withdrawn and then reinstated. Measured as “fill on a successful run” the effect reverses sign; measured as what §9.6 actually pays per attempt it is 1.47×. The effect was real and the precision was never earned — the same fault that withdrew this item’s first 2.2× and F18 beside it.     Geometry is 5% of a generated defence — and designed, it is worth four times as much

    finding Fixed in the document both re-measured

                    off     on    contribution
    generated  30.7%  48.7%  +18.0
    designed   18.0%  100.0%  +82.0

    The generator is the thing to fix, and cheaply. It lays one hedge band with a gap, then scatters three to five clumps of tall grass — and tall grass hides the raider (§12.17), anywhere it lands, including on the route. A good part of what it calls geometry is cover handed to the attacker. A generator that placed the Vault away from the entry, kept one route long, and put cover off the path rather than on it would close most of the gap without any new mechanic.

    G20

    §9.6’s day and week caps do not say whose base they are in, or what “five days’ worth” is five days of

    unspecified Open backend re-measured
    §9.6§24.12

    §9.6: “Per day: the fatigue curve, plus a hard ceiling half again above it for players punching up. Per week: five days’ worth, not seven”. Enforcing them (the server, capHaul) needs three things the sentence leaves out. The fatigue curve is in B(V), and V is the target’s Vault level, which changes raid to raid; a day’s ceiling needs one base. “Five days’ worth” is five days of either the curve or the ceiling, and only the curve makes “grinding every day gains little” true: at five of the ceiling, a player raiding every day at the curve never meets the week’s cap. And nothing says when a week starts.

    §24.1: “Budget: about 100 to 200 kilobytes and five writes per active player per day. That is the design constraint”. Its cost table puts 1,000 and 10,000 monthly players at €0 on free plans, and says the paid plan’s 50 million row writes a month are “several times what a million players generate”. The load test (server/load.mjs, recorded in server/load.json) plays §14.1’s players through the server as built: an engaged player writes at least 46 rows a day, 9.2 times the budget; a regular one 24 and a casual one 10.5. A clean heist in steady state writes about 14 — the lease issued and settled, the heist, up to four ledger lines, Renown on both sides, stars, two ratings, an event batch, the defender’s notification — each of which §24.12, §12.9, §18.2, §12.22 or §13 asks for. So five writes cannot carry one heist, let alone four. A million monthly players, a third of them playing on a day as §25.1’s gate has it, write about 460 million rows a month if engaged and 105 million if casual — 9 and 2 times the 50 million included; at the paid price in §28.3 that is about $416 and $60 a month, not $5 to $15. And a re-simulation takes about 15 ms of CPU (22 ms at the 95th percentile) where §28.3’s free plan allows “10 milliseconds” a request, so the free plan cannot validate a heist at all: the €0 columns need the $5 plan from the first heist. Found by the load test. Re-measured when the landing entered the replay (§5.4): the drawn test player now lands on a drawn edge tile, so a few of its heists end differently, and a heist’s rows moved by 0.01 a player-day; none of the figures above changed. Re-measured again for the owner’s answers: a loud or partial heist now books its fee’s return (C41), a raid past the week’s 20 books nothing (G20) and target lists are rebuilt hourly (G21): an engaged player writes 46.13 rows a day, and a million monthly players cost about $416 a month on the paid plan. G29’s answer, which dates a session by the device, leaves those figures as they were. Re-measured for Keeper levels (G42): each raid now also writes its raider’s level and experience, one row more, so an engaged player writes 50.13 rows a day, ten times the budget, and a million monthly players cost about $456 a month on the paid plan. Counted as D1 bills — every index entry a write touches is a row written too, and the load test now counts them — that day was 103 rows, about $984 a month for a million. Cut without changing a rule: a heist books one ledger row a player, its lines kept in its outcome; a player’s events of a day are one row appended to, an append touching no index; a sign-in is recorded once a day; a lease is settled by its heist row, not written again; and the heists’ index no longer holds whether each was validated. An engaged player now costs 71.8 billed rows a day, 14 times the budget, and a million monthly players about $673 a month engaged, $322 regular and $142 casual. And a cost no figure showed is gone: the heist row was written after the ledger, Renown and star rows that name it, so SQLite searched each of those tables whole on every heist — a read that grew with every heist ever played (22 ms a heist at 300,000 ledger rows, against 11 ms now at any size). A lease request finds the lease a player holds on a target from their newest lease there alone, one row however many they have played (the review of these cuts caught a first version that read every played one). server/test/cost.test.mjs holds each cut.

    → Re-derive §24.1’s budget and cost table from measured writes: state a share of monthly players active on a day, price the writes a heist must make, and drop the free-plan columns for validation. Or cut the writes: settle a heist in one row that holds its ledger lines, Renown and stars, at the price of querying them from JSON.

    ✓ Decided A: Keep the build; re-derive §24.1 from measurement (the build already does this). Document: §24.1, Dynamic tier row: remove 'several times what a million players generate'. Cost table: Infrastructure $5, $5, $5 to about $21, about $60 to $615. Unavoidable cash row: drop 'That is the whole recurring bill' and add the $5 plan. Replace 'The dominant cost of this game is the Apple fee, not its servers. At a million monthly players the infrastructure is about $5 to $15 a month...' with 'The Apple fee is the larger cost below about 100,000 monthly players; above that, database writes are, at about $60 to $615 a month at a million'. Replace 'Where the free tier breaks' with 'The free plan cannot validate a heist (about 15 ms against 10 ms), so the $5 plan is needed from the first heist'. Budget line: the measured rows a heist and a day, with a third of monthly players active on a day. §24.5: the Apple row loses 'the only unavoidable recurring cost'; the infrastructure row becomes '$5 a month from launch; about $60 to $615 at a million monthly players' and loses 'the smaller half of the bill'; 'the servers are not the cost. The Apple fee is.' becomes 'the servers cost $5 a month until the game is large, and then a fraction of a percent of revenue'. §22.5: 'The entire unavoidable bill is $99 a year to Apple and $25 once to Google' gains 'and $5 a month for the database plan'. §27.2's backend row: 'about $5 to $15 a month at a million' becomes 'about $60 to $615 a month at a million', and 'the only unavoidable recurring cost' becomes 'with the $5 database plan, the unavoidable recurring costs'.

    F50

    finding Open backend
    §20.12§24.1

    §20.12: “Erasure completes within thirty days, backups included, with a log kept”. §24.1’s one backup is the database’s own point-in-time restore to any minute of the last 30 days. Restoring to a minute before a deletion brings the account back — identity, push token, telemetry, friends — and takes the log of the deletion with it, since the log is a column of the row it deleted. The server’s reading: every deletion is written first to a journal outside the database (an account id, a reason, a time; nothing that names a person), and every deletion in it is made again when the server starts, before anyone can sign in. The journal must live where a restore of the database does not reach. Found by the privacy inventory. Since the owner’s answer the journal is in object storage, and a start makes again only its last 31 days.

Outside this repository: the bucket the journal lives in, and who may write to it; an export job with a 30-day expiry, if exports are built. Document: §20.12 as A. §24.6 "Lost data" row: "every deletion made in the last 31 days is re-made from the journal, which lives in object storage, whenever the server starts; table exports are kept at most 30 days".

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: the answers stand, and the build’s precedence is stated once: a recorded answer first, then the document, then the design (stage SD, TD.29). The next version takes the answers’ drafted edits (T1.6); §23.2’s Observatory row needs none. If v3.6 meant to reverse an answer, that answer is named, the reversal recorded and the server reverted. The alternatives are the document as written, reverting at least five built answers, or re-deciding the five a screen draws. Meanwhile the Observatory, scout and planner draw each target’s fee from the server and show no scout lock.

    G47

    The heist’s orders are not settled: the abilities, Sage powers and casts §12.7 draws have no command, and the load target, stopping, dropping loot and pausing have no control

    unspecified Open both
    §12.5§12.6§12.7§12.18§12.19§11.2§11.7§15.3§20.8§24.12§24.13

    §12.7 puts the crew portraits, the Sage and a cast on the bottom row, and Screens v3 draws them (screens_main.markup.html:809-820). The simulation has nothing for them to command. Its replay has twelve kinds of command, MoveTo to Land (sim/src/replay.rs:53-110), none for an ability, a Sage power or a cast; the header carries a crew count only, and roles come from a fixed list of five (sim/src/lib.rs:353). Four command values are free. No section says when a cast is paid: §12.5 prices it at “30 Aether per point of the law’s base cost”, and §24.13 says only that “The entry fee is debited at validation, not at lease.”

    And three decisions the heist names have no control in §12.7 or §12.18. §12.6: “The player sets how full they want the crew before it leaves”, but §12.5’s planning table does not list it; the design fixes it at 80% (“Load to 80%”, screens_main.js:98, not tappable), and the build always loads to 100 (client/features/heist/heist_controller.gd:94), though the simulation’s Load takes a percentage. §12.6 names “whether to drop loot to run faster”, §12.19 prices it, and standing still matters in tall grass and under Stillness. The simulation has Halt and Drop, and the build shows Halt and Drop-half buttons beside a gait button (client/scripts/heist_screen.gd:305-309), outside §12.7’s set and against §12.18’s “There is no crawl and no gait button, so the eight-control cap holds”; the design has neither.

    §12.7: “Never more than eight things to tap at once”. Its own Sage and Cast rows open wheels, and the design’s Sage wheel leaves the portraits live, so eleven things are tappable at once (screens_main.js:462, :467). §15.3 opens the law card on request and §20.8 lets the heist be “paused at any time in ruins and rehearsals”, and neither names a control. Nothing says what a heist does when the phone leaves the app: the build simply stops stepping (client/scripts/heist_screen.gd:216-222) and handles no background notice, so a resume may catch up many ticks at once. Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: a simulation task: G51’s crew manifest in the replay, Ability, Sage and Cast commands in the free values, the eighteen abilities as named parameter changes, the four-ready rule and the Archivist’s powers; the harness re-measures §12.6’s decision band; the goldens are regenerated. Then write into §12.5 and §12.18: the load target set in the planner (50 to 100% in tens, the last one used by default) and changed by a held tap on the Vault; a held tap on a crew member offering Stop, Drop half and Drop all, in place of the build’s buttons; wheels and held-tap menus modal, so the cap holds; the law card from a held tap on a law chip; pause in ruins and rehearsals from the clock; a cast paid at validation, only when used. And in §24.12: the simulation pauses with the app and resumes after a three-second count, and a heist left past its lease is submitted as played so far.

    G48

    No rule chooses the result’s decisive moment or its one thing to try, and the simulation keeps no events to find them in

    unspecified Open both
    §12.13§15.3§23.2§24.10

    §12.13: “every heist result names the moment that decided it and what could have been done instead”, with “a three-second replay of it”, and “One thing to try: a single suggestion tied to that moment, never a list.” §23.2 makes both must-shows. Every tip is headed “The Archivist · try this” (screens_main.markup.html:843), which makes it one of §15.3’s Archivist’s tips — “At most one per session; never blocks play; can be turned off” — rather than the result’s own row. Same crew, a bigger haul.”, suggests another target instead of following from its moment (“Your crew crossed the open ledge while the Scout faced away”). Recommended: §12.13 says a Foiled or Partial heist’s moment is the first capture, traced to the tick its captor became Alerted to that crew member; a Loud heist’s, the first guard Alerted and why; a Clean heist’s, the closest call, the tick a guard came nearest to Alerted; and a fault or a law’s blink at that tick is named. Tips come from a content table keyed by cause, never a purchase, in a row labelled “Try this”, not the Archivist’s, each tied to its moment. The alternatives keep the design’s Archivist heading, with §15.3 exempting the result’s tip from its one a session, or ship the design’s fixed moment and tip per outcome. Under any answer sim/ keeps an event log outside the checksum (TD.13); under A and B the device chooses the moment from it (TD.17).

    C47

    v3.6 states three heist and result rules two ways: the worth question’s scale and frequency, what ‘alarm’ means, and whether the Vault’s contents show before it opens

    conflict Open frontend & design
    §19.5§20.3§23.2§22.2§25§12.15§12.9§12.17§12.6§12.12§19.16§12.19§21.8

    The worth question. §19.5 asks “‘Was this worth your time?’, one tap”, “Every session, live”, and reads the fun gate as “‘Worth your time’ at 4.3 out of 5 or higher”; the launch gate in §22.2 and §25 wants at least 4 out of 5. §20.3: “Every session can end with a short summary and a one-tap ‘Was this worth your time?’ rating”, but §23.2 puts it on every heist result. Screens v3 asks “Yes” or “Not really” (screens_main.markup.html:860), which cannot make a five-point average; the server takes 1 to 5 once a session (server/src/telemetry.mjs:49-53, :84). Its reply, “Thanks. It helps us tune the targets you see.” (markup:861), claims what §12.15 rules out: “Nothing is hidden. Targets are drawn by Renown band and the player’s own choice”.

    The word ‘alarm’. §12.9’s Clean is “No alarm; everyone out with loot” and Loud “Alarm raised; everyone out”, and §12.17’s Alerted guard raises the alarm. But the realm’s alarm, the six-level ladder, climbs with time, bodies and bell posts whatever the crew does (§12.6, §12.17), so ‘no alarm’ cannot mean it. The simulation reads §12.9 as a flag set when a guard becomes Alerted, not the ladder (sim/src/lib.rs:701-704, 3177-3181). Screens v3 reads it as the ladder: each alert adds a level (realm_diorama.js:218; screens_main.js:113) under the banner “Alarm +1 · they are looking”, which §12.17 does not have; and its Clean result shows “2:14 · 0 / 6 alarm” (screens_main.js:645), impossible when its own clock adds a level every 30 seconds.

    The Vault’s contents. §12.12: “the Vault’s contents are only revealed when it opens”; §19.16: “A Vault shows its size before its contents”. But §12.6, §12.19 and §21.8 keep “what is left to load” always on screen. The design shows “Left 2,600” from the first second (markup:799), and so does the build (client/scripts/heist_hud.gd:51). Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: ask the worth question as one row of five one-tap points, once a session on a heist result, never required, and make §20.3 and §23.2 agree on when; the reply is “Thanks.” Name §12.9’s condition “no guard alerted” and keep “alarm” for the six-level ladder; the heist says “Seen: this heist is Loud now”, and the result shows the true peak alarm or none. Before the Vault opens, “Left” shows the free rough estimate (§12.4) or “?”, the exact figure once open; amend §12.6’s always-on list to say so. The alternatives are the design’s Yes or Not really with each alert a ladder level, or the five points after every heist.

    G49

    The Codex rests on five things v3.6 never defines: chapter 1’s twelve laws, meeting a law, mastery, Codex notes, and what a player sees of a combination before the Lab names it

    unspecified Open both
    §7.6§14.4§7.8§18.5§14.9§15.3§8.4§8.5§8.6§5.5§23.2

    Chapter 1. §7.6: “at launch it holds the launch 24 (7), 12 findable from the start and all 24 from Keeper level 6”, and “Matchmaking only shows universes running laws from open chapters.” No section names the twelve. content/laws.json has no chapter, the economy model says so and takes the cheapest laws (tools/economy_model/model.py:615-619), and the server has no chapters.

    Meeting a law. §7.6: “The first time a player meets a law it joins the Codex with 1 page.” §14.4 pays it and §7.8 counts “Laws on the route the player has never met”. Meeting is not defined: crossing its realm, being on the route, a scout report, a ruin, or the Archivist. Screens v3 treats a law seen in a scout as still unknown (“Seen in Mira’s Hive”).

    Mastery. §18.5: “One per school, filled by crossing and weaving its laws. Milestones unlock titles and new visual styles for that school’s laws.” Nothing says what fills a track, by how much, or what each milestone gives; §14.9’s goal is a different thing, “Weave and cross every law of one school, at tier III, and win with each”. Screens v3 calls a law at tier III “Mastered” and counts “3 mastered” (screens_meta.js:391, :406), a per-law reading §18.5 does not make. §23.2’s Codex row asks for mastery.

    Codex notes. §15.3: “What the player has seen each law do”, filled in automatically. Nothing defines them, and no design has them.

    Combinations before discovery. Resonances are “hidden until discovered in the Lab, or hinted at after crossing them in someone else’s universe” (§8.4); the Lab names chords (§8.5); §8.6 shows them “Once discovered”. But §5.5 applies a resonance’s ×0.8 and a chord’s ×0.9 and draw whether or not the player knows, so a realm’s strain moves by amounts its owner cannot explain. Screens v3’s Harmony view names them and celebrates “RESONANCE FOUND” or “CHORD FORMED” on first view (screens_meta.js:1080-1081), a way to discover them the document does not have; the client already names them on the owner’s island (client/scripts/builder_screen.gd:204-218). What a crossing hint says is unwritten; the design’s is “You crossed this in Kofi’s universe. Its partner is a Spirit law.” And §8.6’s “the Codex shows how many remain in each school” has no rule for a resonance joining two schools (Mangrove banks is Time and Life); the design shows one total, 2 of 12 (screens_meta.js:406). Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: §7.6 names chapter 1’s twelve, two laws of each school (the ten launch commons with Aurora and Echoes, the three starting laws among them), and defines meeting as a heist or ruin route entering a realm running the law, a scout showing the name and rank but giving no page. §18.5’s track has three steps for each law the school has in play (woven, crossed in a successful heist, raised to tier III), a title at a third of them and at all of them and the school’s new visual style at two thirds: 4, 8 and 12 steps on the four launch laws a school has, 8, 16 and 24 once it has its eight. The screen says ‘Tier III’, not ‘Mastered’. A Codex note records the heists that crossed the law, the pylons broken and the wins with it. §8.6 says an undiscovered resonance or chord in the player’s own realm still sounds and is priced, shown as an unnamed line until the Lab names it; a crossing hint names the partner law’s school; and a two-school resonance counts in each school’s ‘remaining’ and once in the total. The alternatives are the design’s readings, or a Codex without chapters, mastery or notes.

    C48

    Weaving’s upkeep is priced against a realm budget §5.5 never gives, and five more weaving rules are open

    conflict Open both
    §5.6§5.5§29.1§8.2§8.5§5.1§7.6§23.2§19.6

    Upkeep. §5.6: “25% when the realm’s stability budget is fully spent, scaling in proportion to the share actually used”, so “a realm running laws worth half its stability pays 12.5% of what it earns”; §29.1 repeats it. But §5.5: “Stability is how much law a universe can hold”, and capacity and strain belong to the universe. No realm has a stability budget, and a crown law has no realm to charge. F17 covers upkeep’s form, not this term.

    A crown law’s cost. §8.2: “Crown laws count in every realm, so a crown law can harmonise with every realm’s laws. A harmony lowers the stability cost of both laws by 15%”. §5.5 prices each law once, and §8.5’s worked example prices its crown law at the Heart only. Whether a crown law’s discounts and penalties compound across realms, count once, or count realm by realm is not said. Screens v3’s Harmony view gives Kinship a different change in each realm: +25% in Emberreach, ±0% in Skyfield, −10% in Tidehold (screens_meta.js:1066-1086).

    How harmonies count. §8.2: “When two laws in the same realm share a note, they harmonise.” Three laws on one note may make one harmony or three pairs, and two laws sharing two notes (Haste and Frictionless share Flow and Spark) one or two; §8.5’s example fits either. Screens v3’s two screens disagree: Weaving counts each partner once per shared note (screens_main.js:355-356), the Harmony view once per note for every law carrying it (screens_meta.js, evalSet). G25 records the simulation reading a harmony’s effect once a note; this is its cost.

    The first session’s weaves against §5.6’s times are C51’s, which owns the first session.

    Breaking and tier rises. §5.5’s Breaking band says “No new weaving”, not whether a weave may push strain from Cracking into Breaking; Screens v3 refuses it (“Too much strain”, screens_main.js:406). §7.6 prices tiers II and III and §5.6 gives their weave times, but nothing says whether a woven law rises in place or is woven again. Weaving one law as a realm law in several realms, which the design allows, breaks no rule and is adopted under §23.5.

    Recommended laws. §23.2 asks Weaving for “Two or three recommended laws”, §19.6 “with a comparison”; nothing says how they are chosen or what the comparison shows. Screens v3’s deck order — a harmony first, a clash last, then the cheapest (screens_main.js:361) — is one candidate. Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: upkeep on the universe’s share, so §5.6 and §29.1 read the universe’s capacity: every realm pays the upkeep share × (woven laws’ cost ÷ capacity) of its own hourly Aether. A crown law is priced once, by the Heart’s laws, as §8.5’s example does, and a harmony counts once per shared note for every law carrying that note, in §8.2 and §5.5’s formula. A weave that would take strain to 125% or over is refused; a tier rise happens in place; Weaving ranks a law that harmonises first, one that clashes last, then the cheapest, and its comparison shows each candidate’s points, the band after weaving and the harmonies and clashes it would make. The alternatives are each realm’s own share, which cuts upkeep to about a sixth, or the design’s counting.

    G50

    Births have no screen, and naming, a stray’s form and a look changed after hatching have no rule

    unspecified Open backend
    §11.5§11.9§11.10§10.2§9.5§11.3§19.20§20.7§24§23.2§23.5

    Births are a core verb with no screen. §10.2’s Nursery makes “one birth every 6 h; holds 3”; §9.5 prices the nth birth at 100 × 1.3265^(n − 1) Essence; §11.9 weighs the kind, “3 for each law woven in its realm, 2 for the realm's own school and 1 for each crown law”; §11.10 sets the form and, on a tie, “the odds are shown before hatching”; §11.3 rolls two traits; and §19.20: “Naming a ruleborn is offered the first time one hatches, and a free outfit comes with it.” No §23.2 row covers hatching, and the Realm view’s must-show has no births. Screens v3 draws none: FIND A NURSERY ends in a toast, ‘Hatch it in a realm with …’ (screens_meta.js:1205), and so do the roster’s locked tiles.

    Naming has no rule: typed or from a word list, whether a name can change, and who sees it. §20.7 keeps 13-to-15 island names to word lists, and §24’s security row says the game has “no free text”, which a typed name would break. C43 is the island-name half of this.

    A stray’s form has no rule. §11.9: “the surprise strays from heists (14.6) are born under one of the laws the crew crossed”, while §11.10’s form follows the Nursery’s realm; nothing says what form a stray takes, least of all under a law that carries none of Hush, Spark and Echo.

    And Screens v3 lets a player change a form after hatching: the album’s USE THIS LOOK says ‘<note> <kind> is now its look’ (js:1204-1205). §11.10 sets the form at hatching and is silent after it. A form’s look shows its quirk, so if the chosen look reaches heists or a guard post, raiders read a quirk the creature does not have. That changes what a raider sees, which §23.5 does not let a design add. Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: a Hatch row in §23.2 (ready births and the Nursery’s three, the Essence price, the kind’s odds by §11.9’s weights, the form and its odds on a tie, the two traits rolled, and naming); ruleborn names from word lists at every age, changeable and seen only by their owner, the one naming rule C43’s answer set for islands and G58 recommends for Keepers; a heist stray born under one of the laws the crew crossed, drawn evenly, that law’s note setting its form; and USE THIS LOOK not built, the album offering ‘Show mine’. The alternatives are USE THIS LOOK for the portrait only, or typed names kept on the phone.

    G51

    The heist the server re-simulates has five fixed roles at level 1, and the rules for growth, a home and rest it would need are not all written

    unspecified Open both
    §11.4§11.5§11.6§11.3§12.5§12.9§9.6§23.2§14.1

    The Roster and Character screens show each ruleborn’s kind, level, traits and form, and the planner picks a crew and a Sage. None of it reaches the heist the server checks. The simulation’s crew is const CREW: [Role; 5] = [Role::Scout, Role::Breaker, Role::Carrier, Role::Warden, Role::Mender] (sim/src/lib.rs:353), chosen by a count (World::new(_seed, crew: u8, …), :747); sim/src/heist.rs:233-234 says “the simulation has no traits yet”; the replay’s commands (sim/src/replay.rs:53-90) have no ability, Sage or cast; and POST /v1/leases takes a bundle, an owner, a trace flag, a mode and a challenge, and no crew (server/src/http.mjs:492-496). So the server also cannot set each member’s rest (§12.9), which the Roster’s must-show ‘rest timers’ needs.

    Modelling the crew needs four rules v3.6 leaves open:
    Growth — §11.4: “Each level: +8% health and power, +5% carry. Abilities improve at levels 4, 7 and 10”, 20% stronger each time. It does not say the 8% compounds, though the repository reads it so (tools/decision_support.py:298, LEVEL_GROWTH = 1.08), nor which number grows for an ability with two: the Lantern Wisp’s 6 tiles and 6 s, the Featherkin’s 3 tiles and one height, the Echoplate’s 8 s and 40%, the Prism Mite’s 8 s and its halves.
    A home — §11.4: “Highest level = 2 × the level of the Hearth the character lives in”; §11.6: “Hearths shorten rest 5% per level”; §11.5: “The roster holds 3 characters for the Spire plus the places in every Hearth”. The Spire’s three have no Hearth, so no ceiling and no rest cut, and nothing says how a character is housed in a Hearth or moved between them. F56 covers the starting universe only.
    Rest — §12.9’s 45, 60 and 180 minutes, the Hearth’s 5% a level, Loyal’s “rests 25% less after a success” and Sleepy’s “rests 50% longer” combine by no stated rule, and nothing says whether Loyal counts for a member caught in a Partial (a success is any outcome but Foiled, §9.6).
    Reassign — §23.2’s Roster must-show “one-tap reassign” names no destination; Screens v3 sends everyone to a Star Well, in two taps (screens_meta.js:197). G22 asks §14.1 to state the staffing order the pacing assumes, and the one tap should follow it.

    Found reading Screens v3 and the build against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: the lease and the replay carry one crew manifest, each member’s kind, form, level and traits, the Sage and the casts carried, which the server checks against the roster it holds and sim/ models, before the Roster’s and Character’s numbers are shown as the heist’s. G47’s commands and G60’s actors use this manifest. §11.4 to §11.6 state that growth compounds; that a two-number ability’s duration grows, or its reach where it has no duration; that the Spire’s three places count as a home at the Spire’s level and a character moves between free places at no cost; that rest modifiers multiply and Loyal counts a member who got out of a Partial; and one-tap reassign follows G22’s staffing order. The alternatives are the rules now with the crew modelled later, or heists by role only.

    G52

    A heist earns Insight and Sages level with it, and no section says how much any source pays, what the improvements are, or whether a lone Sage may guard

    unspecified Open backend
    §11.7§9.1§9.5§12.5§12.10§14.1§14.3§17.3

    §9.5 prices Sage levels at 15 × 1.13^(level − 1) Insight, up to level 40. §9.1 names Insight’s sources, “Successful heists, Lab discoveries, anomalies”, with no amounts; Echo trials (§12.10) and constellation targets (§17.3) pay it with none either; and §14.1’s “Pages and Insight arrive as described in 7.6 and 11.7” points to two sections that give none. §11.7: “Every fifth level improves one power (an extra use, a longer effect or a shorter cooldown)”, and no Sage’s eight improvements are named. The economy model leaves Sage levels out (tools/economy_model/rerun.py:39 lists “the main Sage's levels (Insight, 11.7)” as not modelled), yet §14.3 prints the day the main Sage reaches levels 10, 20, 30 and 40. The alternatives are Insight amounts for each source in §9.1, from the economy model, paid at settlement and shown on the result, or no Sage levels at all. Under any answer §11.7 says whether a lone Sage may guard rather than go (proposed: yes) and that an at-home effect applies whenever the Sage is not on a heist.

    G53

    The Lab’s hints, its chord naming and what an experiment takes and pays are unwritten, and Screens v3 invents the hint

    unspecified Open backend
    §8.4§8.5§8.6§15.1§15.2§23.2§9.1§7.5§7.6§16§21.5§10.2

    Hints. §23.2’s Lab must show “hints”, and §15.2 lists “Lab hints and "unstable" warnings”, but §8.4 and §8.6 define only the hint a player gets from crossing a resonance in a heist, and §15.1 says “Hints appear only after repeated failure, and every hint is tested before release”. Screens v3 makes its own rule: one failed pair that shares a law with an undiscovered resonance shows that law on the resonance’s card, ‘… now shows one of its two laws’ (screens_meta.js:15-16, 464). That is a hint after one failure, and it changes what a player learns. The design also gives each resonance a settle time its note calls ‘the clue’ (all twelve are 5.5 h today), where §10.2 sets one time per Lab level.

    Chords. §8.5: “The Lab names chords — from level 3 it identifies one the player has woven or crossed”, and §21.5 draws “A third sphere for chords”. Nothing says what starts it, whether it takes a slot, time or Aether, or which chord it names when several qualify. Screens v3 has no chord in the Lab.

    What an experiment takes and pays. Insight from “Lab discoveries” (§9.1) and §16’s “with insight pages” have no amount. §7.6’s “Lab experiments that find nothing give 3 pages of a law from those schools” does not say which law. §7.5: “A universe can hold one paradox at a time”, with no rule for finding a second. Nothing says whether a law not yet restored may go on a pedestal; Screens v3 allows any law met (js:388-389). F37 already asks whether an empty pairing can be re-run for pages.

    Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: after three empty experiments that included the same law, the Lab hints one undiscovered resonance of that law, in the Codex’s one ‘hinted’ state (§8.6); from Lab level 3 the third sphere names, once a day and free, the first chord in §8.5’s table the player has woven or crossed and not yet named; a discovery pays Insight only if G52 keeps it; the 3 pages go to the law the player marked as working on, or else to the first law placed, and only restored laws are placed (§7.6); and while a universe holds a paradox, an unstable pair runs as an ordinary one (§7.5). §23.5 refuses the design’s stir hint and per-resonance times. The alternatives are the document as written, with no Lab hint and no chord naming yet, or the design’s stir hint.

    G54

    Curation swaps a law at once and free, and §13.3 never says whether a swap is a weave

    unspecified Open backend
    §13.3§5.6§7.10

    §13.3 makes “Swap a law” curation’s first verb, and generates the defence “weaving only those of their laws that help the defender”. §5.6: laws are woven in “10 minutes at tier I, 40 minutes at tier II and 2 hours at tier III” at “40 Aether per point of the law's stability cost”, and after a removal “the slot then rests for an hour before it can be woven again”. Screens v3’s Swap and the river’s Across/Along choice apply at once, with no price or timer, priced only in hold (screens_meta.js:540-546, 581). Nothing says whether a curation swap is a weave, and so pays §5.6’s Aether and waits its time, or is exempt; nor whether generating a defence may unweave a law the player wove for production. The player sees both on the screen. F12 covers the eight laws’ placement choices, not this. Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: §13.3 says the curation screen previews any swap at once and free, and applying it weaves the new law at §5.6’s price and time, both shown on the button; re-placing a choice law stays free; and the generator never unweaves, weaving only into empty slots and only laws that help the defender. The alternatives are curation exempt, as the design has it, or priced but instant.

    unspecified Open both
    §13.2§13.3§13.4§18.7§23.2

A curated defence keeps the generated origin while only §13.3’s verbs are used and is authored once its terrain is edited; one outside its band saves with a warning and is judged against its origin’s band. The alternatives are the design’s formula with saving only in band, a batch on the phone, or the count alone.

    G59

    28% of Screens v3’s text fails §21.8’s contrast, and v3.6 does not say how outlined text is measured

    unspecified Open frontend & design re-measured
    §21.8§20.8§23.5

    §21.8: “Contrast meets 4.5:1, checked against a perceptual model as well, because the standard formula overstates contrast on dark backgrounds.” Measured over the 1,049 text runs on Screens v3’s 28 screens, each against the pixels under it with the glyphs made transparent, by the formulas in client/ui/colour_check.gd: 201 (19%) are under 4.5:1 against the median background, 234 (22%) against the worst tenth, 250 (24%) under the perceptual level for their size and weight, and 292 (28%) fail one or the other.

    The causes: white marks on light fills (113 runs, median 2.77:1), 85 of them tab and section badges on red, green or violet at 1.8 to 2.8:1 (screens_main.js:664–665); the law card’s title “Stillness” in white on cyan #81DEEA at 1.55:1; tertiary #8A7AA8, about 4.5:1 but Lc 34; secondary #B8A8D8, 7 to 9:1 but Lc 57 to 59; on parchment #7A5A34 at 3.04:1, #2F7A45 at 3.99:1 and #8A6A4A at 4.22:1; and the heist’s crew names in school colours over the 3D ground at 1.4 to 3.1:1.

    The design leans on 3 to 4.5 px ink strokes and hard ink shadows under its words, and v3.6 does not say whether an outline counts as the background. Counting them would pass 31 of the 201: one run whose outline reads at 4.5:1 against its fill, and 30 whose hard shadow does (the crew names’ shadows read at 5.8 to 10.3:1). The client’s check reads only a StyleBoxFlat’s fill (client/tests/a11y_tests.gd:58–81) and knows neither gradients nor outlines. §23.5 lists text size, not contrast, and D72 covers only the alarm red and the success green. Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: §21.8 says words with an ink outline all round, at least 1.5 points or 12% of their size wide, are measured against the outline, and a drop shadow does not count. The alternatives are outlines never counting, or outlines and hard shadows both counting. The build fixes the rest in the tokens and keeps the look: tertiary text lifted to #B8A8D8 and bold, secondary to #D8CCF2, badges with ink words or on the deep end of their fill, no opacity on words, law titles on a plate; and the check learns the colour each word sits on (TD.3).

    C52

    §21.3 and §24 give different frame-rate floors on different phones, and §24’s 25 ms drag budget cannot be measured or met as written

    conflict Open frontend & design
    §21.3§24§21.1

    §21.3: “Frame rate: 60 frames a second on iPhone 12 and newer, never below 30 on the oldest supported phone.” §24: “60 frames a second is a floor, because 30 measurably harms performance”, on a reference device that is “A mid-range 4 GB Android at 60 Hz, not a flagship”. One section lets old phones fall to 30; the other makes 60 the floor on a mid-range Android.

    §24 also asks for “Under 25 ms from touch to picture for dragging”. One frame at 60 Hz is 16.7 ms; the engine draws after it reads the touch, and Android’s compositor shows the frame at the next refresh, so a drag normally appears two frames or more after the finger moves. Without prediction 25 ms is out of reach. No section says how it is measured, whether prediction counts or what a miss triggers; no client test measures it, and the roadmap’s TC.8 names the figure without a method. Found reading Screens v3 against v3.6.

    → The owner decides (the decision brief). Recommended: one rule naming both tiers, in §24’s reference-device row: 60 a second on the reference device and anything faster, iPhone 12 and newer among them, and never below 30 on the oldest supported phone, which is named; §21.3’s line points to §24. The drag budget is measured touch to picture on the reference device with a high-speed camera, one or two frames of drag prediction allowed; the build reads touches unbatched and late, keeps the 3D frame under about 8 ms, and TC.8 takes the measurement. The alternatives are both lines as written, §24’s device as the one rule, or drag counted inside the engine.

    unspecified Open both

     20–39%  16.5%
     40–59%  23.5%
     60–79%  30.0%
    80–100%   0.0%

    conflict Fixed in the document backend

    waits on F17

    Geometric against linear. Both say owned, so the nth birth is priced at n − 1: at the 10th they are 352 and 460, and at the roster ceiling of 38 they are 17,612 and 1,580, eleven times apart.

    §9.5 is not the self-consistent one, which this item said until it was checked. Its three worked examples — 400, 1,600 and 6,600 — are 405, 1,637 and 6,621: one whole step of the curve above what its own formula gives. The two rows either side of it in the same table write their offsets out, as level − 2 and level − 1; the birth row is the only one in §9.5 that leaves the reader to infer one, and its examples and its formula infer differently. So adopting §9.5 means deciding which of the two is meant, and this item is that decision as much as it is the deletion.

    It matters less than it looks, and that is the finding. Modelled, the roster fills to the Hearth cap of 38 by day 31 under either formula, because Essence income outruns both (F17). A price that cannot bind is not really a price, so this is a tidy-up rather than a balance question — until F17 is fixed, at which point it becomes one.

    → Take §9.5’s, delete §11.5’s sentence, and revisit the growth rate when F17 is settled. If Essence is ever made scarce, the difference between 1,580 and 17,612 at the ceiling is the difference between a roster the player fills and one they build.

    G44

    §24.1 and §26.8 name rate limits, and nothing says how fast a player may ask

    unspecified Open backend re-measured
    §24.1§24.6§26.8§24.2

    §24.1’s moderation is “Deterministic word lists, rate limits, reports and mutes”, and §26.8 lists “rate limits” among the backend’s pieces. §24.6 answers denial of service with “Absorbed at the edge as part of the platform”. The platform absorbs a flood of traffic, but not one signed-in account asking the server, within the platform’s limits, to re-simulate replays (§24.2, about 15 ms of CPU each, F47) or read its tables all day. Every one of those requests is a database read, and some are a simulation. No section gives a figure. The build holds each caller to four token buckets, kept in memory and never in the database, each kind capped on its own: 60 calls at once then two a second by account; six simulations at once then one every 20 seconds by account (an island checked, a replay or a Workshop entry re-simulated); ten sign-ins at once then one every 10 seconds by the account the credential proves; and twenty failed sign-ins at once then one every 3 seconds by address (an IPv6 address by its /64), where the deployment names the header that carries it. Only failures count to an address, so players behind one address are never held by each other. Past a bucket the answer is 429 with Retry-After; the app says it is held back, not offline, keeps its session for its hour rather than signing in each heist, and its outbox tries again later. A refused call is counted from the token’s signature and reads nothing from the database. Each edge isolate keeps its own buckets, so a caller spread across isolates gets more; the platform’s own rate limiting, keyed the same way, holds that. The review of the first version found an IPv6 caller taking a fresh bucket for each address, sign-ins from varied addresses evicting every player’s buckets, sign-ins unlimited without the address header, and players sharing an address refused; all are fixed. Found in the security briefing.

    → State in §24.1 how fast a player may ask and what is limited by address, or accept the build’s figures; and bind the platform’s rate limiting to the same keys when the edge is deployed.

    Decisions that are yours

    These cannot be resolved by reading the document more carefully — they change what the game is. Each says what it blocks, what the numbers are, and a leaning where there is one. Q8 is small and comes first: it swings Q1 by a factor of three.

    Q1

    Is character scarcity a feature or an accident?

    decision Fixed in the document backend
    §4§11.5§5.2§9.3

    waits on Q8 · unblocks C19, C27, Q4

    F1 shows 152 positions against a roster of 38. §4 claims characters' time is one of the game's two scarce resources, which would make this deliberate. But 25% coverage is not an allocation puzzle, and §9.3's production figures assume staffing the roster cannot supply.

    → Blocks: Q4, C19, the economy spec, and every pacing date in §14.
    The numbers (decision_support.py staffing): 152 positions against a roster of 38; only 12 characters free to work once guards and a crew are committed; no second or third worker slot is ever worth filling, though §10.2 grants them at building levels 4 and 7; and two independent caps — Hearth homes and §9.5's birth curve — both say 30–40 without referring to each other.
    Depends on Q8: if a Guardian Post holds more than one ruleborn, defence alone consumes 42–63 characters and the shortage stops being severe and becomes absolute.
    No recommendation. This is a design choice about whether scarcity is the point. What is not a choice is leaving all three tables as they are.

    v3.0 Answered by §5.8: scarcity is a feature.

    Q2

    Should the raid-versus-build trade-off be made real, or dropped?

    decision Fixed in the document backend
    §4§11.6§12.9

    F3 shows it is worth about 2% of production. It can be made real by making crew membership exclude work the way guarding does, or the claim can be removed from §4 and §11.6. What it cannot do is stay as written.

    → Blocks: nothing technical, but it decides whether §4's central claim survives.
    The numbers: a crew of five raiding four times a day is withheld from work for 16 character-hours out of 744 — about 2% of production.
    Leaning: make crew membership exclude work the way guarding does, so five of 38 are committed rather than 0.67. The scarcity needed already exists in F1; it is simply not connected to raiding. Lengthening rest instead runs against §12.14's rule that failure stays temporary.

    v3.0 Answered by §5.8: crew membership excludes work, so the trade-off binds.

    Never stated anywhere in the document, and it is the missing conversion between §5.2, which counts guard posts, and §13.4, which counts guards — one post against three guards at realm level 1, three posts against six at level 5, so no constant reconciles them. §10.2's Guardian Post entry gives the post's capability per level (“guard +10% health and sight”) but never a capacity.

    → Blocks: C5, and it swings Q1 by a factor of three.
    Leaning: one. It matches §9.2's phrasing, keeps §5.2's numbers intact, and keeps defence affordable against the roster. Anything higher means F1's arithmetic has to be redone first, because defence would then consume more characters than production.
    A small question with a large blast radius — worth answering before Q1, not after.

That was never stated anywhere, and it is the missing conversion between counting posts and counting guards — without it the two tables could not be reconciled and defence could have consumed more characters than production.” §13.4. That is exactly what this decision asked for, including why it mattered.

    How this page is maintained. The register lives in tools/audit_register.py and this page is generated by python3 tools/build_audit.py. Change an item's status there and rebuild — never edit the generated HTML, or the next build will overwrite it.

    Findings marked F were produced by tools/economy_model/, which rebuilds the day-by-day model §24 describes but does not contain. Contradictions marked C are asserted where possible in tools/check_design_consistency.py, so they are re-checked automatically against any later version of the document rather than by re-reading 85,000 words.
